We connect intertwiner groups to a model's internal representations of data through a range of experiments that probe similarities between hidden states across models with the same architecture. Our work suggests that the symmetries of a network are propagated into the symmetries in that network's representation of data, providing us with a better understanding of how architecture affects the learning and prediction process. Finally, we speculate that for ReLU networks, the intertwiner groups may provide a justification for the common practice of concentrating model interpretability exploration on the activation basis in hidden layers rather than arbitrary linear combinations thereof.

papers.title: Analysis of Fourier Neural Operators via Effective Field Theory
papers.research_question: How can we provide a principled explanation for the stability, generalization, and frequency behavior of Fourier Neural Operators? The paper investigates this using effective field theory.
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a systematic effective field theory analysis of Fourier Neural Operators, deriving closed recursion relations for the kernel and four-point vertex, and proposes a calibration procedure for initialization that improves optimization stability and test error.
papers.conclusion: The effective field theory framework quantifies how nonlinearity enables neural operators to capture non-trivial features and supplies criteria for hyperparameter selection, explaining the benefits of scale-invariant activations and residual connections.
papers.key_findings:
Nonlinear activations inevitably couple frequency inputs to high frequency modes, even with spectral truncation.
Criticality conditions on weight initialization ensure small input perturbations maintain uniform scale across depth.
Scale-invariant activations and residual connections enhance feature learning in FNOs.
The proposed calibration procedure leads to more stable optimization, faster convergence, and improved test error on the PDEBench Burgers benchmark.
papers.limitation: The theory is primarily valid at initialization and during the early stage of training.
papers.abstract: Fourier Neural Operators (FNOs) have emerged as leading surrogates for solver operators for various functional problems, yet their stability, generalization and frequency behavior lack a principled explanation. We present a systematic effective field theory analysis of FNOs in an infinite-dimensional function space, deriving closed recursion relations for the layer kernel and four-point vertex and then examining three practically important settings-analytic activations, scale-invariant cases and architectures with residual connections. The theory shows that nonlinear activations inevitably couple frequency inputs to high frequency modes that are otherwise discarded by spectral truncation, and experiments confirm this frequency transfer. For wide networks, we derive explicit criticality conditions on the weight initialization ensemble that ensure small input perturbations maintain a uniform scale across depth, and we confirm experimentally that the theoretically predicted ratio of kernel perturbations matches the measurements. Taken together, our results quantify how nonlinearity enables neural operators to capture non-trivial features, supply criteria for hyperparameter selection via criticality analysis, and explain why scale-invariant activations and residual connections enhance feature learning in FNOs. Finally, we translate the criticality theory into a practical criterion-matched initialization (calibration) procedure; on a standard PDEBench Burgers benchmark, the calibrated FNO exhibits markedly more stable optimization, faster convergence, and improved test error relative to a vanilla FNO.

papers.title: A Toy Model of Universality: Reverse Engineering How Networks Learn Group Operations
papers.research_question: The paper investigates the universality hypothesis: whether different models learn similar features and circuits when trained on similar tasks, by studying how small neural networks learn to implement group composition.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the group composition via representations (GCR) algorithm and shows that neural networks consistently learn this algorithm when trained on group composition tasks, providing evidence for weak universality (underlying principles exist) but against strong universality (specific circuits vary).
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that while there is an underlying algorithm (GCR) that networks learn for group composition, the specific features and circuits are arbitrary, supporting weak universality but not strong universality.
papers.key_findings:
Networks learn the GCR algorithm for group composition, which uses representation theory to compute compositions.
The specific representations (circuits) learned vary across different runs and hyperparameters, indicating that while the algorithm is universal, the implementation is not.
The order in which representations are learned is arbitrary and not consistent across runs.
The network's logits can be approximated as a sum of characters from a sparse set of representations.
Ablations confirm that the identified components are causally important for the task.
papers.limitation: The algorithm does not perfectly explain all logits due to limitations of the architecture (e.g., ReLU activations imperfectly implement matrix multiplication).
future_direction: Extending to other group theoretic tasks such as conjugacy, group actions, and automata.
Studying semigroups (which lack representation theory).
Investigating inductive biases of networks more broadly.
papers.abstract: Universality is a key hypothesis in mechanistic interpretability -- that different models learn similar features and circuits when trained on similar tasks. In this work, we study the universality hypothesis by examining how small neural networks learn to implement group composition. We present a novel algorithm by which neural networks may implement composition for any finite group via mathematical representation theory. We then show that networks consistently learn this algorithm by reverse engineering model logits and weights, and confirm our understanding using ablations. By studying networks of differing architectures trained on various groups, we find mixed evidence for universality: using our algorithm, we can completely characterize the family of circuits and features that networks learn on this task, but for a given network the precise circuits learned -- as well as the order they develop -- are arbitrary.

papers.title: Exploring explicit coarse-grained structure in artificial neural networks
papers.research_question: How can hierarchical coarse-grained structure be explicitly employed in neural networks to improve interpretability without degrading performance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces hierarchical coarse-grained structure into neural networks to improve interpretability without degrading performance, via TaylorNet for classification and a multi-level data distillation setup.
papers.conclusion: The hierarchical coarse-grained structure improves interpretability without degrading performance, and TaylorNet and the distillation setup are effective.
papers.key_findings:
TaylorNet achieves 99.2% accuracy on MNIST and 71.7% on CIFAR-10 with fewer parameters than some baseline models.
Coarse-grained operations in TaylorNet are more powerful than convolution operations for representing nonlinear mappings.
The multi-level data distillation process captures essential features of the dataset, and distilled images can be used as references for classification.
Weight distribution analysis shows that dominant terms in Taylor expansion are local.
The hierarchical coarse-grained structure makes neural networks more understandable while maintaining acceptable performance.
papers.limitation:
The loss function in distillation could be designed more smartly.
The partition of the dataset and choice of hyperparameter λ might affect the distillation results.
The fixed point of the scale transformations is not discussed.
future_direction: Using multiple TaylorNets with orthogonality constraints for higher efficiency.
Studying fixed points of scale transformations in TaylorNet and the iterative distillation procedure.
papers.abstract: We propose to employ the hierarchical coarse-grained structure in the artificial neural networks explicitly to improve the interpretability without degrading performance. The idea has been applied in two situations. One is a neural network called TaylorNet, which aims to approximate the general mapping from input data to output result in terms of Taylor series directly, without resorting to any magic nonlinear activations. The other is a new setup for data distillation, which can perform multi-level abstraction of the input dataset and generate new data that possesses the relevant features of the original dataset and can be used as references for classification. In both cases, the coarse-grained structure plays an important role in simplifying the network and improving both the interpretability and efficiency. The validity has been demonstrated on MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets. Further improvement and some open questions related are also discussed.

papers.title: Rapid Identification of X-ray Diffraction Spectra Based on Very Limited Data by Interpretable Convolutional Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can a convolutional neural network be trained with limited experimental data to achieve rapid one-to-one identification of X-ray diffraction spectra?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a CNN model trained on noise-augmented theoretical XRD spectra for rapid one-to-one identification of individual materials, achieving 96.7% Top-5 accuracy and providing interpretability through class activation maps.
papers.conclusion: The CNN model enables accurate one-by-one identification of XRD spectra using noise-augmented data and provides interpretability through CAMs, with potential applications in various characterization techniques.
papers.key_findings:
The CNN model achieves 96.7% Top-5 accuracy for identifying 1012 MOFs from XRD spectra.
Noise-based data augmentation from experimental spectra enables effective training with limited data.
Neighborhood components analysis shows that XRD spectra from the same material cluster together.
Class activation maps reveal that the CNN focuses on main peaks for identification, similar to expert analysis.
The model is robust to peak shifts, intensity variations, and noise when combined with filtering techniques.
papers.limitation: Lower crystallinity and high noise in experimental spectra can reduce classification accuracy.
future_direction: Expanding the method to other characterization techniques such as Raman, NMR, and FTIR.
papers.abstract: Large volumes of data from material characterizations call for rapid and automatic data analysis to accelerate materials discovery. Herein, we report a convolutional neural network (CNN) that was trained based on theoretic data and very limited experimental data for fast identification of experimental X-ray diffraction (XRD) spectra of metal-organic frameworks (MOFs). To augment the data for training the model, noise was extracted from experimental spectra and shuffled, then merged with the main peaks that were extracted from theoretical spectra to synthesize new spectra. For the first time, one-to-one material identification was achieved. The optimized model showed the highest identification accuracy of 96.7% for the Top 5 ranking among a dataset of 1012 MOFs. Neighborhood components analysis (NCA) on the experimental XRD spectra shows that the spectra from the same material are clustered in groups in the NCA map. Analysis on the class activation maps of the last CNN layer further discloses the mechanism by which the CNN model successfully identifies individual MOFs from the XRD spectra. This CNN model trained by the data-augmentation technique would not only open numerous potential applications for identifying XRD spectra for different materials, but also pave avenues to autonomously analyze data by other characterization tools such as FTIR, Raman, and NMR.

papers.title: Building Data-driven Models with Microstructural Images: Generalization and Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can convolutional neural networks be used for classifying microstructure with a focus on generalization between data sets, number of features required, and interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that the mean texture featurization of pre-trained CNN outputs is a simple, generalizable, and interpretable method for classifying microstructural images, and that using features from multiple convolutional layers improves performance.
papers.conclusion: The mean texture featurization of CNN outputs is a generalizable and interpretable method for SEM image classification, and visualization of texture features provides insights into the model's decision-making and the differentiating aspects of various microstructures.
papers.key_findings:
The mean texture featurization strategy performed well across three different SEM image datasets, is computationally efficient, and does not require updating a dictionary when new images are added.
Model performance strongly depends on which convolutional layer features are extracted from, with optimal layers varying by dataset; using features from all five layers together provided at least as good or better performance than any single layer.
The texture features can be visualized via gradient ascent to show the input patterns that maximally activate specific convolutional filters, providing interpretability into what the model uses for classification.
For the steel dataset, the most important texture features for the random forest classifier corresponded to dotted patterns, which visually mimic the spheroidite microstructure, showing the model prioritized distinguishing spheroidite from other categories.
Characteristic textures for each microstructure category (e.g., network, spheroidite, pearlite) can be identified and visualized, reflecting the visual differences between the categories.
papers.limitation: A missing link is the availability of multiple sizable public datasets that contain both SEM images and corresponding material properties, which are needed to extend the featurization techniques to predict properties directly.
future_direction: Evaluating the featurization techniques on datasets for which material properties are also available to predict properties from SEM images.
Using the visualization techniques to determine which textures are characteristic of favorable mechanical properties.
papers.abstract: As data-driven methods rise in popularity in materials science applications, a key question is how these machine learning models can be used to understand microstructure. Given the importance of process-structure-property relations throughout materials science, it seems logical that models that can leverage microstructural data would be more capable of predicting property information. While there have been some recent attempts to use convolutional neural networks to understand microstructural images, these early studies have focused only on which featurizations yield the highest machine learning model accuracy for a single data set. This paper explores the use of convolutional neural networks for classifying microstructure with a more holistic set of objectives in mind: generalization between data sets, number of features required, and interpretability.

papers.title: A Quantitative Approach to Predicting Representational Learning and Performance in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we predict the kinds of representations learned by a neural network and the resulting downstream performance from the initial conditions and training curriculum?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a pseudo-kernel based method (combining NTK and ideas from Sahs et al.) to predict the inductive bias, representational learning, and downstream performance of neural networks from initial conditions and training curriculum.
papers.conclusion: The paper introduces a method to predict inductive bias, representational learning, and downstream performance from initial conditions and training curriculum, highlighting the trade-off between flexibility (shared representations) and efficiency (separated representations).
papers.key_findings:
The proposed method (using NTK/PNTK) can predict the evolution of representations in a linear network, validating against known theoretical results.
Standard (small) weight initialization promotes shared representations, which improve generalization but hinder concurrent multitasking performance.
Large weight initialization promotes separated representations, which improve concurrent multitasking performance but hinder generalization.
The NTK analysis at initialization can predict the clustering of representations that emerges during training, as visualized by M-PHATE.
The method quantitatively predicts the trade-off between flexibility (shared representations) and efficiency (separated representations) in neural networks.
papers.limitation: The approach is currently limited to feedforward networks and simple tasks.
future_direction: Extend the method to more complex architectures and tasks.
Apply the method to understand learning and processing in biological neural networks.
papers.abstract: A key property of neural networks (both biological and artificial) is how they learn to represent and manipulate input information in order to solve a task. Different types of representations may be suited to different types of tasks, making identifying and understanding learned representations a critical part of understanding and designing useful networks. In this paper, we introduce a new pseudo-kernel based tool for analyzing and predicting learned representations, based only on the initial conditions of the network and the training curriculum. We validate the method on a simple test case, before demonstrating its use on a question about the effects of representational learning on sequential single versus concurrent multitask performance. We show that our method can be used to predict the effects of the scale of weight initialization and training curriculum on representational learning and downstream concurrent multitasking performance.

papers.title: Enhancing Multimodal Large Language Models Complex Reason via Similarity Computation
papers.research_question: How can the complex reasoning ability of Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) be improved by efficiently utilizing image information and filtering out irrelevant image tokens?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that image tokens semantically related to text have information flow convergence and higher attention scores in the LLM decoder, and proposes Simignore, a method to filter irrelevant image tokens based on similarity computation, which improves complex reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: The proposed Simignore method, which computes similarity between image and text embeddings to filter irrelevant tokens, enhances the complex reasoning ability of LVLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Image tokens semantically related to text prompts are more likely to have information flow convergence and receive higher attention scores in the LLM decoder.
Filtering out irrelevant image tokens based on similarity between image and text embeddings improves the accuracy of LVLMs on complex reasoning tasks.
The performance improvement depends on the number of tokens ignored, with an optimal number (e.g., 124 out of 576 for LLaVA1.5-7B) yielding the best results.
Important image tokens (with high similarity to text) are crucial for complex reasoning, while unimportant tokens can be ignored to improve performance and reduce computation.
Cosine similarity performs better than Euclidean and Manhattan distance for computing the similarity between image and text embeddings in this task.
papers.limitation:
The method does not adaptively choose the number of image tokens to ignore.
The internal mechanisms of how image and textual information work together to facilitate complex reasoning are not fully understood.
future_direction: Exploring strategies for adaptively choosing the number of image tokens to ignore.
Investigating the internal mechanisms of the model to more fully understand how image and textual information work together.
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models have experienced rapid growth, and numerous different models have emerged. The interpretability of LVLMs remains an under-explored area. Especially when faced with more complex tasks such as chain-of-thought reasoning, its internal mechanisms still resemble a black box that is difficult to decipher. By studying the interaction and information flow between images and text, we noticed that in models such as LLaVA1.5, image tokens that are semantically related to text are more likely to have information flow convergence in the LLM decoding layer, and these image tokens receive higher attention scores. However, those image tokens that are less relevant to the text do not have information flow convergence, and they only get very small attention scores. To efficiently utilize the image information, we propose a new image token reduction method, Simignore, which aims to improve the complex reasoning ability of LVLMs by computing the similarity between image and text embeddings and ignoring image tokens that are irrelevant and unimportant to the text. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method for complex reasoning tasks.

papers.title: Insights Into the Inner Workings of Transformer Models for Protein Function Prediction
papers.research_question: How can explainable AI methods be extended to inspect latent representations in transformer models for protein function prediction, and do the identified relevant sequence parts reflect biological expectations?
papers.core_contribution: Extends integrated gradients to compute head-specific attributions in transformers for protein function prediction, showing that attribution maps correlate with biological sequence annotations and identifying specialized heads.
papers.conclusion: The extended integrated gradients method provides insights into transformer models for protein function prediction, showing that models focus on biologically relevant sequence parts and that specific heads are specialized for certain annotations.
papers.key_findings:
Attribution maps at the embedding layer correlate significantly with UniProt annotations for EC classes and GO membrane term.
Inside the model, specific transformer heads show significant correlation between attributions and annotations, indicating specialization.
For GO membrane term, heads with positive relevance and correlation with transmembrane regions are identified.
For GO catalytic activity, heads correlate with active sites and PROSITE patterns.
The method is sensitive to model parameters and provides insights beyond anecdotal evidence.
papers.limitation: The method may identify significant heads due to coincidental partial alignment of randomly initialized heads with directions in feature space that happen to correlate with sequence annotations.
papers.abstract: Motivation: We explored how explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) can help to shed light into the inner workings of neural networks for protein function prediction, by extending the widely used XAI method of integrated gradients such that latent representations inside of transformer models, which were finetuned to Gene Ontology term and Enzyme Commission number prediction, can be inspected too. Results: The approach enabled us to identify amino acids in the sequences that the transformers pay particular attention to, and to show that these relevant sequence parts reflect expectations from biology and chemistry, both in the embedding layer and inside of the model, where we identified transformer heads with a statistically significant correspondence of attribution maps with ground truth sequence annotations (e.g. transmembrane regions, active sites) across many proteins. Availability and Implementation: Source code can be accessed at https://github.com/markuswenzel/xai-proteins .

papers.title: Network Dissection: Quantifying Interpretability of Deep Visual\n Representations
papers.research_question: How can interpretability of deep visual representations be quantified, and what factors affect the emergence of interpretable units in CNNs?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework called Network Dissection for quantifying the interpretability of latent representations in CNNs by evaluating the alignment between individual hidden units and a broad set of semantic concepts.
papers.conclusion: Network dissection provides a method to quantify interpretability in CNNs, revealing that interpretability is not an inevitable result of discriminative power and is affected by network architecture, training data, and training techniques.
papers.key_findings:
Interpretability is not axis-independent; random rotations of the representation destroy interpretability, indicating it is a property of the learned basis.
Interpretability varies with network architecture and depth, with ResNet showing the highest number of unique concept detectors.
Supervised training on scene-centric data (Places) yields more object detectors than object-centric data (ImageNet), while self-supervised models produce more texture detectors.
Batch normalization significantly decreases interpretability, while dropout removal increases texture detectors but decreases object detectors.
Widening the convolutional layer (increasing units) can increase the number of interpretable concept detectors without significantly harming classification accuracy.
papers.limitation: Network dissection works only as well as the underlying dataset; if a unit matches a human-understandable concept that is absent in Broden, then it will not score well for interpretability.
future_direction: Finding ways to capture the benefits of batch normalization without destroying interpretability.
Expanding Broden to include more kinds of visual concepts.
papers.abstract:
We propose a general framework called Network Dissection for quantifying the
interpretability of latent representations of CNNs by evaluating the alignment
between individual hidden units and a set of semantic concepts. Given any CNN
model, the proposed method draws on a broad data set of visual concepts to
score the semantics of hidden units at each intermediate convolutional layer.
The units with semantics are given labels across a range of objects, parts,
scenes, textures, materials, and colors. We use the proposed method to test the
hypothesis that interpretability of units is equivalent to random linear
combinations of units, then we apply our method to compare the latent
representations of various networks when trained to solve different supervised
and self-supervised training tasks. We further analyze the effect of training
iterations, compare networks trained with different initializations, examine
the impact of network depth and width, and measure the effect of dropout and
batch normalization on the interpretability of deep visual representations. We
demonstrate that the proposed method can shed light on characteristics of CNN
models and training methods that go beyond measurements of their discriminative
power.

papers.title: TabPFN Through The Looking Glass: An interpretability study of TabPFN and its internal representations
papers.research_question: How does TabPFN, a tabular foundational model, process and transform input features? What information is encoded in its hidden representations and how do these representations evolve across layers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that TabPFN encodes intermediate and final quantities of simple arithmetic tasks in its hidden representations in a linearly decodable manner, suggesting the model performs structured, hierarchical computation internally.
papers.conclusion: TabPFN implements systematic, hierarchical computation, with intermediate results linearly represented in the residual stream, moving towards more interpretable and trustworthy tabular foundation models.
papers.key_findings:
Linear regression coefficients can be linearly decoded from the model's hidden states within a single model fit, but not across different fits.
Intermediate arithmetic terms (e.g., a*b) are linearly decodable from middle-layer activations, indicating the model respects the order of operations.
The final answer can be decoded from hidden states earlier in the network (layer 5) than it is correctly projected to the output space via the logit lens (layer 8).
Input values and their linear combinations can be decoded from the activations of the answer token early in the model, suggesting a copying mechanism.
The model does not maintain a fixed, universal encoding of coefficients across different fits; representations are fit-specific.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to simple arithmetic (additive/multiplicative) toy expressions, unlike the highly complex, noisy functions found in real-world datasets.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to more complex, real-world functions.
Using mechanistic interpretability methods like activation patching to find the mechanisms through which the answer is computed.
Manipulating the function through steering vectors or vector ablation.
papers.abstract: Tabular foundational models are pre-trained models designed for a wide range of tabular data tasks. They have shown strong performance across domains, yet their internal representations and learned concepts remain poorly understood. This lack of interpretability makes it important to study how these models process and transform input features. In this work, we analyze the information encoded inside the model's hidden representations and examine how these representations evolve across layers. We run a set of probing experiments that test for the presence of linear regression coefficients, intermediate values from complex expressions, and the final answer in early layers. These experiments allow us to reason about the computations the model performs internally. Our results provide evidence that meaningful and structured information is stored inside the representations of tabular foundational models. We observe clear signals that correspond to both intermediate and final quantities involved in the model's prediction process. This gives insight into how the model refines its inputs and how the final output emerges. Our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the internal mechanics of tabular foundational models. They show that these models encode concrete and interpretable information, which moves us closer to making their decision processes more transparent and trustworthy.

papers.title: Prototype-Based Interpretable Graph Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can prototype-based interpretable networks (ProtoPNet and TesNet) be adapted to the graph domain for graph and node classification, and do these adapted models provide interpretability while maintaining or improving performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper adapts prototype-based interpretable networks (ProtoPNet and TesNet) to graph neural networks, demonstrating that these models can achieve equal or better classification performance than black-box counterparts while providing intrinsic interpretability through prototype activations.
papers.conclusion: Prototype-based models can be successfully adapted to the graph domain for interpretable graph and node classification, providing a basis for future development of interpretable graph neural network architectures.
papers.key_findings:
Adapted ProtoPNet and TesNet models, especially TesNet with GIN backbone, often outperform their black-box counterparts on graph and node classification tasks.
The proposed k-hop method for visualizing prototype activations provides clearer explanations without sacrificing fidelity.
The interpretable models produce more faithful explanations (higher Fidelity+) than post-hoc methods and other self-explainable models like ProtGNN and SEGNN.
Transfer learning does not provide advantages in this setting, likely due to differences in graph domains (domain of applicability).
The number of prototypes per class is a hyperparameter that requires tuning, but no general pattern was found across datasets.
papers.limitation:
Transfer learning does not work well due to differences in graph domains (domain of applicability).
The number of prototypes is a hyperparameter that needs to be tuned.
future_direction: Investigate the use of metrics better tailored to the graph domain.
Develop methods to automatically modulate the number of prototypes learned by the model.
Further development of interpretable graph architectures.
papers.abstract: Graph neural networks have proved to be a key tool for dealing with many problems and domains such as chemistry, natural language processing and social networks. While the structure of the layers is simple, it is difficult to identify the patterns learned by the graph neural network. Several works propose post-hoc methods to explain graph predictions, but few of them try to generate interpretable models. Conversely, the topic of the interpretable models is highly investigated in image recognition. Given the similarity between image and graph domains, we analyze the adaptability of prototype-based neural networks for graph and node classification. In particular, we investigate the use of two interpretable networks, ProtoPNet and TesNet, in the graph domain. We show that the adapted networks manage to reach better or higher accuracy scores than their respective black-box models and comparable performances with state-of-the-art self-explainable models. Showing how to extract ProtoPNet and TesNet explanations on graph neural networks, we further study how to obtain global and local explanations for the trained models. We then evaluate the explanations of the interpretable models by comparing them with post-hoc approaches and self-explainable models. Our findings show that the application of TesNet and ProtoPNet to the graph domain produces qualitative predictions while improving their reliability and transparency.

papers.title: Neuron-based explanations of neural networks sacrifice completeness and interpretability
papers.research_question: Do neuron-based explanation methods sacrifice completeness and interpretability compared to activation principal components for networks like AlexNet?
papers.core_contribution: For AlexNet, principal component analysis (PCA) of activations provides a more complete and interpretable basis for explaining network function than the standard neuron basis.
papers.conclusion: PCA-based explanations are more complete and interpretable than neuron-based explanations for AlexNet, suggesting that population-level analysis (like dimensionality reduction) is beneficial for neural network explainability.
papers.key_findings:
Principal components (PCs) account for much of the activation variance with far fewer vectors than neurons, indicating a more efficient basis.
Ablating high-variance PCs generally degrades AlexNet's validation accuracy more than ablating high-variance neurons (except in the first convolutional layer).
In a user study, visualizations of high-variance PCs were rated as more interpretable (coherent) than visualizations of high-variance neurons.
The neuron basis disregards the distributed nature of representations and is less complete and interpretable for most layers of AlexNet.
Small-eigenvalue PCs are generally uninterpretable and have a smaller effect on accuracy when ablated.
papers.limitation:
The study mainly focuses on AlexNet pretrained on ImageNet, potentially limiting the generality of the claims to other networks or datasets.
There are cases where neuron-based explanations might be useful, such as in the first and final layers of a network.
The user study tests a low threshold for interpretability (coherence of transitions), which provides limited insight into deep network function.
The study only analyzes the forward pass, not the backward pass (gradients).
future_direction: Extending the comparison of neuron and PCA-based explanations to other networks and datasets.
Studying the backward pass (gradients) using similar dimensionality reduction and visualization techniques.
Exploring non-linear dimensionality reduction methods to capture non-linear manifolds in activation space.
papers.abstract: High quality explanations of neural networks (NNs) should exhibit two key properties. Completeness ensures that they accurately reflect a network's function and interpretability makes them understandable to humans. Many existing methods provide explanations of individual neurons within a network. In this work we provide evidence that for AlexNet pretrained on ImageNet, neuron-based explanation methods sacrifice both completeness and interpretability compared to activation principal components. Neurons are a poor basis for AlexNet embeddings because they don't account for the distributed nature of these representations. By examining two quantitative measures of completeness and conducting a user study to measure interpretability, we show the most important principal components provide more complete and interpretable explanations than the most important neurons. Much of the activation variance may be explained by examining relatively few high-variance PCs, as opposed to studying every neuron. These principal components also strongly affect network function, and are significantly more interpretable than neurons. Our findings suggest that explanation methods for networks like AlexNet should avoid using neurons as a basis for embeddings and instead choose a basis, such as principal components, which accounts for the high dimensional and distributed nature of a network's internal representations. Interactive demo and code available at https://ndey96.github.io/neuron-explanations-sacrifice.

papers.title: Interpretability and Generalization Bounds for Learning Spatial Physics
papers.research_question: How does the function space of training data affect the generalization of machine learning models when learning linear differential equations, and can learned models be interpreted in terms of Green's functions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that generalization in learning spatial physics depends critically on the function space of the training data, and introduces a cross-validation technique and a mechanistic interpretability lens based on extracting Green's functions from learned models.
papers.conclusion: Learning spatially dependent problems is limited by the underlying function space of the training data, and careful data selection and cross-validation are needed; different model classes exhibit opposing generalization behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
Learned parameters in finite difference models converge with error depending on grid spacing and polynomial order of data.
Linear models only converge to a projection of the true operator onto the subspace of the training data, limiting out-of-distribution generalization.
Deep models and SciML models (DeepONet, Neural Operator) do not always generalize out-of-distribution.
Physics-informed losses (PINNs, PI-DeepONet) suffer from the same subspace limitation as black-box models.
Green's function operators can be extracted from black-box models when they generalize effectively across test domains.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical analysis requires a priori knowledge of how the dataset was constructed.
Real-world data collection has inherent limitations that may hinder discovering unknown physics.
future_direction: Develop new methods capable of discovering the underlying subspace of the data to compensate for limitations.
Use cross-set generalization as an evaluation benchmark for future differential equation learning techniques.
papers.abstract: While there are many applications of ML to scientific problems that look promising, visuals can be deceiving. Using numerical analysis techniques, we rigorously quantify the accuracy, convergence rates, and generalization bounds of certain ML models applied to linear differential equations for parameter discovery or solution finding. Beyond the quantity and discretization of data, we identify that the function space of the data is critical to the generalization of the model. A similar lack of generalization is empirically demonstrated for commonly used models, including physics-specific techniques. Counterintuitively, we find that different classes of models can exhibit opposing generalization behaviors. Based on our theoretical analysis, we also introduce a new mechanistic interpretability lens on scientific models whereby Green's function representations can be extracted from the weights of black-box models. Our results inform a new cross-validation technique for measuring generalization in physical systems, which can serve as a benchmark.

papers.title: Enhancing Pre-trained Representation Classifiability can Boost its Interpretability
papers.research_question: Can classifiability-oriented pre-trained representations achieve high interpretability and classifiability simultaneously?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers a positive correlation between interpretability and classifiability in pre-trained vision representations, introduces the Inherent Interpretability Score (IIS) to quantify representation interpretability, and shows that improving one can mutually promote the other.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability and classifiability are mutually promoting for classifiability-oriented pre-trained representations, allowing practitioners to unify improvements in both aspects for vision models.
papers.key_findings:
Interpretability and classifiability of pre-trained representations are positively correlated, not conflicting.
Representations with higher classifiability contain more interpretable semantics that can be captured in interpretations.
Fine-tuning pre-trained models with an interpretability maximization objective (simplified IIS) can further improve their classifiability on downstream tasks.
Predictions based on the interpretations of high-classifiability representations suffer less accuracy degradation compared to the original representations.
The mutual promoting relationship provides a new pathway for interpretable representation learning.
papers.limitation:
Investigations of the underlying mechanism leading to the positive correlation between interpretability and classifiability have not been conducted.
The method fine-tunes representations by maximizing a simplified version of IIS, not the original IIS.
future_direction: Investigate the underlying mechanisms of the observed positive correlation between interpretability and classifiability.
Better integrate the Inherent Interpretability Score (IIS) into the training process of pre-trained models.
papers.abstract: The visual representation of a pre-trained model prioritizes the classifiability on downstream tasks, while the widespread applications for pre-trained visual models have posed new requirements for representation interpretability. However, it remains unclear whether the pre-trained representations can achieve high interpretability and classifiability simultaneously. To answer this question, we quantify the representation interpretability by leveraging its correlation with the ratio of interpretable semantics within the representations. Given the pre-trained representations, only the interpretable semantics can be captured by interpretations, whereas the uninterpretable part leads to information loss. Based on this fact, we propose the Inherent Interpretability Score (IIS) that evaluates the information loss, measures the ratio of interpretable semantics, and quantifies the representation interpretability. In the evaluation of the representation interpretability with different classifiability, we surprisingly discover that the interpretability and classifiability are positively correlated, i.e., representations with higher classifiability provide more interpretable semantics that can be captured in the interpretations. This observation further supports two benefits to the pre-trained representations. First, the classifiability of representations can be further improved by fine-tuning with interpretability maximization. Second, with the classifiability improvement for the representations, we obtain predictions based on their interpretations with less accuracy degradation. The discovered positive correlation and corresponding applications show that practitioners can unify the improvements in interpretability and classifiability for pre-trained vision models. Codes are available at https://github.com/ssfgunner/IIS.

papers.title: On Interpretability of Deep Learning based Skin Lesion Classifiers using Concept Activation Vectors
papers.research_question: Does a deep learning based skin lesion classifier learn and utilize human-understandable disease-related concepts similar to those used by dermatologists?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a novel training and significance testing paradigm for Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs) and demonstrates that a skin lesion classifier learns and uses human-understandable disease-related concepts similar to those used by dermatologists.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that deep learning based skin lesion classifiers learn and use human-understandable concepts similar to those used by dermatologists, increasing confidence in such CAD systems. The proposed method using identically distributed images for CAV training is effective.
papers.key_findings:
Concept classifiers trained on network activations achieve significantly higher validation accuracies than random baseline, indicating that the latent space encodes human-understandable concepts.
TCAV scores show that disease-related concepts influence predictions in a way consistent with medical knowledge: benign concepts positively affect Naevi class and negatively affect Melanoma, while malignant concepts do the opposite.
The model's use of concepts aligns with dermatological criteria, e.g., atypical pigment network, irregular streaks, regression structures, etc., are positively associated with Melanoma.
The method can sort test images by concept visibility, providing per-image explanations.
The novel training paradigm using identically distributed data for CAV training is effective for skin lesion classification.
papers.limitation: Subjective annotations by experts and small number of concept training samples limit thorough analysis of all concepts.
future_direction: Curating high-quality datasets with reliable fine-grained concept labels.
Extending the approach to unsupervised concept discovery to eliminate the need for expert annotations.
papers.abstract: Deep learning based medical image classifiers have shown remarkable prowess in various application areas like ophthalmology, dermatology, pathology, and radiology. However, the acceptance of these Computer-Aided Diagnosis (CAD) systems in real clinical setups is severely limited primarily because their decision-making process remains largely obscure. This work aims at elucidating a deep learning based medical image classifier by verifying that the model learns and utilizes similar disease-related concepts as described and employed by dermatologists. We used a well-trained and high performing neural network developed by REasoning for COmplex Data (RECOD) Lab for classification of three skin tumours, i.e. Melanocytic Naevi, Melanoma and Seborrheic Keratosis and performed a detailed analysis on its latent space. Two well established and publicly available skin disease datasets, PH <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> and derm7pt, are used for experimentation. Human understandable concepts are mapped to RECOD image classification model with the help of Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs), introducing a novel training and significance testing paradigm for CAVs. Our results on an independent evaluation set clearly shows that the classifier learns and encodes human understandable concepts in its latent representation. Additionally, TCAV scores (Testing with CAVs) suggest that the neural network indeed makes use of disease-related concepts in the correct way when making predictions. We anticipate that this work can not only increase confidence of medical practitioners on CAD but also serve as a stepping stone for further development of CAV-based neural network interpretation methods.

papers.title: Interpretability in Linear Brain Decoding
papers.research_question: What is a formal definition for interpretability of linear brain decoding models, and how can we quantitatively evaluate interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a formal definition for interpretability of linear brain decoding models and proposes a multi-objective criterion combining interpretability and performance for model selection.
papers.conclusion: The proposed definition provides a theoretical background for the quantitative evaluation of interpretability in linear brain decoding.
papers.key_findings:
In noisy data, the most accurate linear decoding model is not necessarily the most interpretable, highlighting a trade-off between performance and interpretability.
Incorporating the proposed interpretability measure into model selection can lead to more interpretable models when using regularization techniques like Lasso.
papers.limitation:
The definition of interpretability is theoretical and assumes the true solution of the brain decoding problem is available, which is not realistic in practice.
The definition and quantification are limited to linear models; extending to non-linear models requires future research.
future_direction: Extending the definition of interpretability to non-linear models.
papers.abstract: Improving the interpretability of brain decoding approaches is of primary interest in many neuroimaging studies. Despite extensive studies of this type, at present, there is no formal definition for interpretability of brain decoding models. As a consequence, there is no quantitative measure for evaluating the interpretability of different brain decoding methods. In this paper, we present a simple definition for interpretability of linear brain decoding models. Then, we propose to combine the interpretability and the performance of the brain decoding into a new multi-objective criterion for model selection. Our preliminary results on the toy data show that optimizing the hyper-parameters of the regularized linear classifier based on the proposed criterion results in more informative linear models. The presented definition provides the theoretical background for quantitative evaluation of interpretability in linear brain decoding.

papers.title: Transformers and the representation of biomedical background knowledge
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether transformer-based models encode biomedical domain knowledge at entity and relational levels, how they handle complex facts, differences between models, and their response to evidence biases in the literature.
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that transformer-based models encode biomedical knowledge, but fine-tuning can lose some semantic structure, and it highlights risks of misclassification due to dataset biases.
papers.conclusion: Transformers encode biomedical knowledge useful for inference, but careful evaluation is needed due to biases and information loss during fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers like BioBERT and BioMegatron encode biomedical domain knowledge at entity and relational levels.
Fine-tuning for specific tasks can lead to loss of semantic information about entity types.
Clustering analysis shows that representations form biologically meaningful groups, such as genes from the same pathways.
Classification errors are correlated with the frequency of entities in the training data, indicating bias.
Despite strong evidence, some well-known clinical relations can be misclassified by the models.
papers.limitation: Models may misclassify well-known clinical relations due to biases in the dataset.
papers.abstract: Specialised transformers-based models (such as BioBERT and BioMegatron) are adapted for the biomedical domain based on publicly available biomedical corpora. As such, they have the potential to encode large-scale biological knowledge. We investigate the encoding and representation of biological knowledge in these models, and its potential utility to support inference in cancer precision medicine - namely, the interpretation of the clinical significance of genomic alterations. We compare the performance of different transformer baselines; we use probing to determine the consistency of encodings for distinct entities; and we use clustering methods to compare and contrast the internal properties of the embeddings for genes, variants, drugs and diseases. We show that these models do indeed encode biological knowledge, although some of this is lost in fine-tuning for specific tasks. Finally, we analyse how the models behave with regard to biases and imbalances in the dataset.

papers.title: A Mathematical Philosophy of Explanations in Mechanistic Interpretability -- The Strange Science Part I.i
papers.research_question: What is the nature of explanations in mechanistic interpretability? How can we define mechanistic interpretability and what are its inherent limits?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a philosophical framework for mechanistic interpretability, including the Explanatory View Hypothesis, a definition of mechanistic interpretability as producing Model-level, Ontic, Causal-Mechanistic, and Falsifiable explanations, and the Principle of Explanatory Optimism.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that if the Principle of Explanatory Optimism holds, interpretability could enable humans to understand machine knowledge, making it a crucial scientific endeavor for the future of human understanding.
papers.key_findings:
The Explanatory View Hypothesis posits that neural networks contain implicit explanations of their behavior that can be extracted and understood.
Explanatory Faithfulness is defined as the extent to which an explanation matches the model's internal ur-explanations, and is well-defined under the Explanatory View.
Mechanistic Interpretability is defined as the practice of producing Model-level, Ontic, Causal-Mechanistic, and Falsifiable explanations of neural networks.
Mechanistic Interpretability has inherent limits, such as theory-ladenness and the potential for high explanatory complexity that may make models incomprehensible to humans.
The Principle of Explanatory Optimism, which states that the algorithmic structure of generalizing neural networks is human-understandable, is a necessary precondition for the success of Mechanistic Interpretability.
papers.limitation:
Mechanistic interpretability may be limited by the theory-ladenness of observations, where the interpreter's prior theories influence what they can discover.
There is a risk that the explanatory complexity of models might be too high for humans to understand, which would make mechanistic interpretability intractable.
future_direction: Formalize the conjectures of Strong and Weak Explanatory Optimism, including defining explanatory complexity classes and explanatory universality.
Prove the formalized conjectures to assess the truth value of the Principle of Explanatory Optimism.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability aims to understand neural networks through causal explanations. We argue for the Explanatory View Hypothesis: that Mechanistic Interpretability research is a principled approach to understanding models because neural networks contain implicit explanations which can be extracted and understood. We hence show that Explanatory Faithfulness, an assessment of how well an explanation fits a model, is well-defined. We propose a definition of Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) as the practice of producing Model-level, Ontic, Causal-Mechanistic, and Falsifiable explanations of neural networks, allowing us to distinguish MI from other interpretability paradigms and detail MI's inherent limits. We formulate the Principle of Explanatory Optimism, a conjecture which we argue is a necessary precondition for the success of Mechanistic Interpretability.

papers.title: Cascade of phase transitions in the training of energy-based models
papers.research_question: How does the Restricted Boltzmann Machine learn features from data, and does it undergo phase transitions during training?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that RBMs learn features through a cascade of second-order phase transitions, each corresponding to the acquisition of a new principal mode of the data distribution.
papers.conclusion: The learning of RBMs occurs through a cascade of phase transitions, providing insight into the feature encoding process in generative models.
papers.key_findings:
The weights grow exponentially in the direction of the principal components of the dataset.
When the weight norm reaches a critical value, the model undergoes a second-order phase transition, splitting the probability distribution into modes.
These phase transitions are in the mean-field universality class, as confirmed by finite-size scaling.
The learning process involves a cascade of such transitions, progressively refining the learned distribution.
The same phenomena are observed in real datasets like MNIST, CelebA, and HGD.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is primarily for RBMs and simplified models; extending to more complex models like Convolutional EBMs is not straightforward.
The Binary-Gaussian RBM cannot reproduce higher-order correlations in data.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to other generative models such as Convolutional Energy-Based Models.
Investigating the implications of phase transitions for training strategies and sampling.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we investigate the feature encoding process in a prototypical energy-based generative model, the Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM). We start with an analytical investigation using simplified architectures and data structures, and end with numerical analysis of real trainings on real datasets. Our study tracks the evolution of the model's weight matrix through its singular value decomposition, revealing a series of phase transitions associated to a progressive learning of the principal modes of the empirical probability distribution. The model first learns the center of mass of the modes and then progressively resolve all modes through a cascade of phase transitions. We first describe this process analytically in a controlled setup that allows us to study analytically the training dynamics. We then validate our theoretical results by training the Bernoulli-Bernoulli RBM on real data sets. By using data sets of increasing dimension, we show that learning indeed leads to sharp phase transitions in the high-dimensional limit. Moreover, we propose and test a mean-field finite-size scaling hypothesis. This shows that the first phase transition is in the same universality class of the one we studied analytically, and which is reminiscent of the mean-field paramagnetic-to-ferromagnetic phase transition.

papers.title: Statistical Physics of Deep Neural Networks: Generalization Capability, Beyond the Infinite Width, and Feature Learning
papers.research_question: This thesis investigates three interconnected questions: (1) Can we derive an improved asymptotic bound on the generalization performance of DNNs? (2) How do DNNs behave in a thermodynamic limit where the number of training examples scales with the number of neurons per layer? (3) Do DNNs truly learn dataset features or merely memorize them?
papers.core_contribution: This thesis contributes three main results: (1) an improved asymptotic bound on generalization error that depends only on the last layer size, (2) a statistical mechanics framework for DNNs in a proportional regime beyond the infinite width limit, linking them to Student's t-processes, and (3) a task-explicit analysis showing conditions under which DNNs learn dataset features rather than memorizing.
papers.conclusion: The thesis demonstrates that statistical physics methods can provide significant insights into the generalization, behavior in proportional regimes, and feature learning of DNNs, contributing to more interpretable AI.
papers.key_findings:
An asymptotic generalization bound that depends only on the last layer size, improving classical statistical learning theory bounds.
A closed formula for the generalization error of a finite-width one-hidden layer network in the proportional regime.
An approximate expression for the partition function of deep neural networks in the proportional regime.
A link between deep neural networks in the proportional regime and Student's t-processes.
Evidence that DNNs can learn dataset features rather than memorizing, as shown by analyzing the volume of the solution space and Gaussianity breaking.
papers.abstract: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) excel at many tasks, often rivaling or surpassing human performance. Yet their internal processes remain elusive, frequently described as "black boxes." While performance can be refined experimentally, achieving a fundamental grasp of their inner workings is still a challenge. Statistical Mechanics has long tackled computational problems, and this thesis applies physics-based insights to understand DNNs via three complementary approaches. First, by averaging over data, we derive an asymptotic bound on generalization that depends solely on the size of the last layer, rather than on the total number of parameters -- revealing how deep architectures process information differently across layers. Second, adopting a data-dependent viewpoint, we explore a finite-width thermodynamic limit beyond the infinite-width regime. This leads to: (i) a closed-form expression for the generalization error in a finite-width one-hidden-layer network (regression task); (ii) an approximate partition function for deeper architectures; and (iii) a link between deep networks in this thermodynamic limit and Student's t-processes. Finally, from a task-explicit perspective, we present a preliminary analysis of how DNNs interact with a controlled dataset, investigating whether they truly internalize its structure -- collapsing to the teacher -- or merely memorize it. By understanding when a network must learn data structure rather than just memorize, it sheds light on fostering meaningful internal representations. In essence, this thesis leverages the synergy between Statistical Physics and Machine Learning to illuminate the inner behavior of DNNs.

papers.title: Discovering Symbolic Models from Deep Learning with Inductive Biases
papers.research_question: How can we combine deep learning and symbolic regression to extract interpretable symbolic models from neural networks, specifically Graph Neural Networks, to discover physical laws and improve generalization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework that combines deep learning (specifically Graph Neural Networks with strong inductive biases) and symbolic regression to distill interpretable symbolic models from neural networks, enabling the discovery of physical laws and improving generalization.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework successfully distills symbolic, interpretable models from Graph Neural Networks, recovers known physical laws, discovers new formulas in cosmology, and improves generalization, offering a promising direction for interpreting deep learning models and advancing scientific discovery.
papers.key_findings:
The method can extract known physical equations (e.g., force laws and Hamiltonians) from the learned representations of Graph Neural Networks.
Applied to a cosmology dataset, the framework discovered a new analytic formula for predicting dark matter halo concentration from the mass distribution of nearby structures.
The extracted symbolic expressions generalized to out-of-distribution data better than the original Graph Neural Network model.
The framework demonstrates that neural networks can learn representations that are linear transformations of true physical quantities (e.g., forces) when appropriate inductive biases are applied.
The approach offers a pathway to interpret neural networks and discover novel physical principles from the representations they learn.
future_direction: Extending the framework to gridded PDE data using existing symbolic regression packages for PDEs.
Using other symbolic regression packages (e.g., PySR, grammar-based methods) as drop-in replacements for eureqa in the framework.
papers.abstract: We develop a general approach to distill symbolic representations of a learned deep model by introducing strong inductive biases. We focus on Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). The technique works as follows: we first encourage sparse latent representations when we train a GNN in a supervised setting, then we apply symbolic regression to components of the learned model to extract explicit physical relations. We find the correct known equations, including force laws and Hamiltonians, can be extracted from the neural network. We then apply our method to a non-trivial cosmology example-a detailed dark matter simulation-and discover a new analytic formula which can predict the concentration of dark matter from the mass distribution of nearby cosmic structures. The symbolic expressions extracted from the GNN using our technique also generalized to out-of-distribution data better than the GNN itself. Our approach offers alternative directions for interpreting neural networks and discovering novel physical principles from the representations they learn.

papers.title: Convolutional neural networks can identify brain interactions involved in decoding spatial auditory attention
papers.research_question: Can a convolutional neural network (CNN) be designed to learn task-specific interactions between brain regions from source-reconstructed EEG data to decode spatial auditory attention, rather than being used as a black box decoder?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an interpretable CNN architecture that learns pairwise interactions between brain regions from source-reconstructed EEG data to decode spatial auditory attention, and demonstrates that this model identifies known important neural interactions and frequency bands.
papers.conclusion: The CNN model can effectively utilize features known to be important in auditory attention tasks, suggesting that domain knowledge-inspired CNNs applied to source-reconstructed EEG data offer a novel computational framework for studying task-relevant brain interactions.
papers.key_findings:
The CNN model achieved median decoding accuracies of 77.56% (within-participant) and 65.14% (cross-participant) for spatial auditory attention.
Analysis of the model's spatial filters revealed alpha-band-dominated inter-hemisphere interactions and alpha- and beta-band dominant interactions that were hemisphere-specific or showed contrasting patterns between hemispheres.
These interactions were more pronounced in parietal and central regions for within-participant decoding, and in parietal, central, and partly frontal regions for cross-participant decoding.
Ablation analysis showed that parietal, temporal, and central brain regions are important for decoding performance.
Removing alpha and beta frequency bands from the input data significantly decreased model performance, indicating their key role.
papers.limitation:
The CNN architecture may not be deep enough to capture longer temporal structures (e.g., delta and theta frequencies), and increasing depth could lead to overfitting due to limited data.
Decoding performance varied across participants, which may be related to the relatively low number of trials per participant and the small overall number of participants.
The use of 64-channel EEG for source reconstruction may yield less precise localization compared to high-density EEG or MEG systems.
future_direction: Future research may use more data, employ data augmentation techniques, utilize more flexible CNN architectures, and/or include behavioral data to account for inter-individual heterogeneity.
Future studies may explore other architectures to adapt the model to brain dynamics, such as incorporating attention layers or graph convolutional neural networks.
Future work could develop a CNN model that integrates both stimulus information (e.g., speech envelopes) and EEG signals to decode auditory attention and study entrainment mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Human listeners have the ability to direct their attention to a single speaker in a multi-talker environment. The neural correlates of selective attention can be decoded from a single trial of electroencephalography (EEG) data. In this study, leveraging the source-reconstructed and anatomically-resolved EEG data as inputs, we sought to employ CNN as an interpretable model to uncover task-specific interactions between brain regions, rather than simply to utilize it as a black box decoder. To this end, our CNN model was specifically designed to learn pairwise interaction representations for 10 cortical regions from five-second inputs. By exclusively utilizing these features for decoding, our model was able to attain a median accuracy of 77.56% for within-participant and 65.14% for cross-participant classification. Through ablation analysis together with dissecting the features of the models and applying cluster analysis, we were able to discern the presence of alpha-band-dominated inter-hemisphere interactions, as well as alpha- and beta-band dominant interactions that were either hemisphere-specific or were characterized by a contrasting pattern between the right and left hemispheres. These interactions were more pronounced in parietal and central regions for within-participant decoding, but in parietal, central, and partly frontal regions for cross-participant decoding. These findings demonstrate that our CNN model can effectively utilize features known to be important in auditory attention tasks and suggest that the application of domain knowledge inspired CNNs on source-reconstructed EEG data can offer a novel computational framework for studying task-relevant brain interactions.

papers.title: The Cognitive Revolution in Interpretability: From Explaining Behavior to Interpreting Representations and Algorithms
papers.research_question: How can we understand, interpret, and explain the behavior of complex intelligent AI systems like large language models, and how can mechanistic interpretability be grounded in cognitive science?
papers.core_contribution: The paper grounds mechanistic interpretability in cognitive science, proposing a taxonomy that categorizes interpretation methods into semantic interpretation (what latent representations are learned) and algorithmic interpretation (what operations are performed over representations).
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that a cognitive revolution in deep learning interpretability is underway, shifting from explaining behavior to interpreting representations and algorithms, and calls for a unified framework that integrates semantic and algorithmic interpretation.
papers.key_findings:
Current interpretability methods are ripe for a transition echoing the 'cognitive revolution' in psychology, shifting from pure behaviorism to studying internal representations and processing.
A taxonomy mirroring computational neuroscience distinguishes semantic interpretation (studying latent representations) and algorithmic interpretation (studying operations and algorithms).
Semantic interpretation methods include optimization and search, structural probing, causal probing, and dictionary learning, each with distinct assumptions and challenges.
Algorithmic interpretation focuses on circuit discovery, using interventions like knockouts and patching to understand the role of sub-networks in model behavior.
The paper discusses parallels and distinctions between approaches, analyzes strengths and weaknesses, and outlines challenges and the possibility of a unified framework.
future_direction: Unifying semantic and algorithmic interpretation under a common framework.
Addressing challenges in scalability, evaluation, and the Rashomon effect in causal analysis.
Developing automated and scalable methods for feature interpretation and evaluation in dictionary learning.
papers.abstract: Artificial neural networks have long been understood as "black boxes": though we know their computation graphs and learned parameters, the knowledge encoded by these weights and functions they perform are not inherently interpretable. As such, from the early days of deep learning, there have been efforts to explain these models' behavior and understand them internally; and recently, mechanistic interpretability (MI) has emerged as a distinct research area studying the features and implicit algorithms learned by foundation models such as large language models. In this work, we aim to ground MI in the context of cognitive science, which has long struggled with analogous questions in studying and explaining the behavior of "black box" intelligent systems like the human brain. We leverage several important ideas and developments in the history of cognitive science to disentangle divergent objectives in MI and indicate a clear path forward. First, we argue that current methods are ripe to facilitate a transition in deep learning interpretation echoing the "cognitive revolution" in 20th-century psychology that shifted the study of human psychology from pure behaviorism toward mental representations and processing. Second, we propose a taxonomy mirroring key parallels in computational neuroscience to describe two broad categories of MI research, semantic interpretation (what latent representations are learned and used) and algorithmic interpretation (what operations are performed over representations) to elucidate their divergent goals and objects of study. Finally, we elaborate the parallels and distinctions between various approaches in both categories, analyze the respective strengths and weaknesses of representative works, clarify underlying assumptions, outline key challenges, and discuss the possibility of unifying these modes of interpretation under a common framework.

papers.title: Beyond Scaling Curves: Internal Dynamics of Neural Networks Through the NTK Lens
papers.research_question: How does scaling model size and dataset size affect the internal dynamics of neural networks, and at what model width does the transition to kernel-like behavior occur?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uses NTK analysis to show that scaling model size and data size have opposite effects on internal dynamics (effective rank and NTK trace) despite similar loss scaling exponents, and identifies the model width at which feature learning diminishes, which is far below typical LLM widths.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that NTK analysis reveals fundamental differences in internal dynamics between model and data scaling, and identifies a transition width for feature learning that is below typical LLM widths, highlighting the need to go beyond loss scaling to understand neural network behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Scaling model size increases the effective rank and initial NTK trace, while scaling dataset size decreases the effective rank and increases the adaptation rate.
The transition from feature-driven to kernel-driven scaling occurs at a model width much smaller than typical large language model widths.
The effective rank dynamics reveal stages of learning that depend on data complexity, with more complex data slowing the evolution.
The trace ratio (relative change in NTK trace) declines with model width, indicating approach to the kernel regime.
For deep networks, the transition points in trace ratio and effective rank coincide, marking the maximum width for feature learning.
papers.limitation:
The results focus on the low-data and small-model regimes, and may not generalize to scenarios where model and data have similar complexity.
Breaking down dynamics into two observables (trace and effective rank of the NTK) may not be sufficient to capture the full complexity of the learning process.
The analysis relies on comparing NTK quantities at specific points in training (initialization and minimum test loss), which may not hold in regimes closer to the interpolation threshold.
future_direction: Consider the effect of depth in future studies to understand kernel-like behavior in state-of-the-art models.
Extend the studied observables to capture all aspects of neural network dynamics for a comprehensive scaling theory.
papers.abstract: Scaling laws offer valuable insights into the relationship between neural network performance and computational cost, yet their underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this work, we empirically analyze how neural networks behave under data and model scaling through the lens of the neural tangent kernel (NTK). This analysis establishes a link between performance scaling and the internal dynamics of neural networks. Our findings of standard vision tasks show that similar performance scaling exponents can occur even though the internal model dynamics show opposite behavior. This demonstrates that performance scaling alone is insufficient for understanding the underlying mechanisms of neural networks. We also address a previously unresolved issue in neural scaling: how convergence to the infinite-width limit affects scaling behavior in finite-width models. To this end, we investigate how feature learning is lost as the model width increases and quantify the transition between kernel-driven and feature-driven scaling regimes. We identify the maximum model width that supports feature learning, which, in our setups, we find to be more than ten times smaller than typical large language model widths.

papers.title: Revealing structure components of the retina by deep learning networks
papers.research_question: What types of network structure components can be revealed by CNNs when they are used to model the single retinal ganglion cell (RGC) response?
papers.core_contribution: CNNs trained to predict neural responses of single retinal ganglion cells learn convolutional filters that resemble biological subunits in the retinal circuit, suggesting CNNs can reveal structural components of neuronal circuits.
papers.conclusion: CNNs can learn interpretable parameters that correspond to biological underpinnings, and this approach can be used to reveal network structure components in neuroscience.
papers.key_findings:
The CNN model can predict the receptive field of retinal ganglion cells well.
The learned convolutional filters in CNN resemble the subunits in the RGC model.
For biological RGC data, the learned conv filters converge to localized subunits comparable to bipolar cells.
The features represented by these filters tile the receptive field of the RGC.
