Our method provides a highly accurate prediction of density functional theory calculated properties for eight different properties of crystals with various structure types and compositions after being trained with 10^{4} data points. Further, our framework is interpretable because one can extract the contributions from local chemical environments to global properties. Using an example of perovskites, we show how this information can be utilized to discover empirical rules for materials design.

papers.title: Peering inside the black box: Learning the relevance of many-body functions in Neural Network potentials
papers.research_question: How can machine learned coarse-grained potentials based on graph neural networks be interpreted in terms of physically meaningful many-body contributions to the total energy?
papers.core_contribution: Extends GNN-LRP to interpret coarse-grained neural network potentials, showing the learned energy can be decomposed into physically meaningful many-body contributions.
papers.conclusion: GNN-LRP provides a way to interpret machine learned coarse-grained potentials, showing the learned interactions are physically meaningful and offering insights into molecular systems.
papers.key_findings:
For methane and water, 2-body relevance scores show repulsive interactions at short distances and, for water, stabilizing interactions at the first solvation shell.
3-body interactions are crucial for water to recover structural properties, with relevance scores indicating stabilizing and destabilizing contributions.
For protein NTL9, relevance scores identify stabilizing interactions in the folded state and can distinguish between two folding pathways.
The method can analyze the effect of mutations by changing bead embeddings, showing the model learns amino-acid specific interactions.
Different GNN architectures (PaiNN and SO3Net) learn similar underlying physical interactions despite different functional representations.
future_direction: Refining the concepts to provide greater insight and systematic choice of architecture and functionalization.
papers.abstract: Machine learned potentials are becoming a popular tool to define an effective energy model for complex systems, either incorporating electronic structure effects at the atomistic resolution, or effectively renormalizing part of the atomistic degrees of freedom at a coarse-grained resolution. One of the main criticisms to machine learned potentials is that the energy inferred by the network is not as interpretable as in more traditional approaches where a simpler functional form is used. Here we address this problem by extending tools recently proposed in the nascent field of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) to coarse-grained potentials based on graph neural networks (GNN). We demonstrate the approach on three different coarse-grained systems including two fluids (methane and water) and the protein NTL9. On these examples, we show that the neural network potentials can be in practice decomposed in relevance contributions to different orders, that can be directly interpreted and provide physical insights on the systems of interest.

papers.title: Occupancies vs Embeddings: Internal representations of Ab Initio and Graph Probabilistic Models*
papers.research_question: To what degree does the end-to-end data-driven approach (graph neural networks) coalesce with traditional ab initio predictions of molecular behavior? Does the model contain internal characteristics of the wave function or electron density from DFT?
papers.core_contribution: This study compares atomwise representations from graph neural networks (GNNs) and ab initio density functional theory (DFT), revealing that GNN embeddings offer higher resolution and can accurately predict DFT-derived atomic occupancy values, whereas the reverse mapping is significantly less accurate.
papers.conclusion: GNN embeddings serve as a richer, more informative molecular representation than DFT-derived atomic occupancies, demonstrating the power of end-to-end statistical models to encapsulate and extend traditional quantum chemical information, though further exploration is needed regarding their robustness beyond equilibrium structures.
papers.key_findings:
Both GNN embedding vectors and DFT-derived atomic occupancy vectors can separate and label chemical environments, but embeddings provide much higher resolution and lower classification error.
Embedding vectors can predict atomic occupancy values with high accuracy (MAE 2.5e-3, R2 0.996), but the reverse mapping from occupancies to embeddings is an order of magnitude less accurate (MAE 0.235, R2 0.379).
Principal Component Analysis (PCA) reveals qualitative similarities in the eigenvalue spectra between the two representations, but the embedding space captures more nuanced information.
The embedding representation contains more information than the occupancy representation, enabling precise mapping to occupancies but not vice versa within the same model chemistry.
Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) shows embeddings achieve near-perfect functional group classification, while occupancy vectors show higher error, especially for similar chemical environments.
papers.limitation: Interatomic information was omitted due to the need to respect rotational equivariance for the embeddings, and the use of Mulliken population analysis might hamper a faithful analysis of the information content in the occupancies.
future_direction: Further studies to tighten conclusions about the relationship between embeddings and electron density.
Exploration of GNN embeddings' robustness beyond equilibrium structures.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Chemical modeling has traditionally been separated into two fairly non-overlapping frameworks: the exact framework of \textit{ab initio} models and the data-driven framework of statistical models. However, recent advances in machine learning approaches have intercepted the exact \textit{ab initio} frameworks by using an \textit{end-to-end} probabilistic model of the Schr\"odinger equation in the Born-Oppenheimer approximation---from raw nuclear configurations to quantum observables such as the energy. While probabilistic modelling offers promising advancements to speed up computational predictions, the internal representation and its connection to the underlying quantum data---the wave function or electron density---which they implicitly rely on for training, remains relatively poorly understood. This study seeks to make a first comparison of the internal representation from a probabilistic end-to-end models with those from pure \textit{ab initio} frameworks such as density functional theory. We do this by comparing the internal atomwise representation of graph models, also called embeddings, to their most natural \textit{ab initio} counterpart, electron occupancy values. Our findings show that the embedding representations can be employed to transfer learn atomic occupancy values whereas the reverse mapping appears to be less accurate. We discuss the assumption that the probabilistic model could infer the existence of an underlying electron density underpinning the computational \textit{ab-initio} data.

papers.title: Beyond Converging Representations A Philosophical Response on the Interpretation Risks of Scientific Foundation Models
papers.research_question: Do scientific foundation models of different modalities, architectures, and training data learn similar internal representations of matter?
papers.core_contribution: Representations learned by nearly sixty scientific foundation models across string-, graph-, 3D atomistic, and protein-based modalities are highly aligned, and they converge as model performance improves, suggesting a common underlying representation of physical reality.
papers.conclusion: Representational alignment serves as a quantitative benchmark for foundation-level generality in scientific models, and current models remain limited by training data and inductive biases.
papers.key_findings:
Models trained on different input modalities (e.g., string encodings and 3D coordinates) show significant representational alignment.
As models improve in energy prediction performance, their representations converge towards those of the best-performing models.
Local (CKNNA) and global (dCor) alignment metrics show consistent trends, indicating robust representational similarity.
Intrinsic dimensionality (Id) of embeddings is consistent across models for a given dataset, suggesting a universal low-dimensional structure.
For in-distribution data, high-performing models align closely while weak models diverge; for out-of-distribution data, most models collapse to a low-information representation.
papers.limitation: Today's models remain limited by training data and inductive bias and do not yet encode truly universal structure.
future_direction: Using representational alignment as a quantitative benchmark for foundation-level generality in scientific models.
Tracking the emergence of universal representations of matter as models scale.
Selecting and distilling models whose learned representations transfer best across modalities, domains of matter, and scientific tasks.
papers.abstract: Machine learning models of vastly different modalities and architectures are being trained to predict the behavior of molecules, materials, and proteins. However, it remains unclear whether they learn similar internal representations of matter. Understanding their latent structure is essential for building scientific foundation models that generalize reliably beyond their training domains. Although representational convergence has been observed in language and vision, its counterpart in the sciences has not been systematically explored. Here, we show that representations learned by nearly sixty scientific models, spanning string-, graph-, 3D atomistic, and protein-based modalities, are highly aligned across a wide range of chemical systems. Models trained on different datasets have highly similar representations of small molecules, and machine learning interatomic potentials converge in representation space as they improve in performance, suggesting that foundation models learn a common underlying representation of physical reality. We then show two distinct regimes of scientific models: on inputs similar to those seen during training, high-performing models align closely and weak models diverge into local sub-optima in representation space; on vastly different structures from those seen during training, nearly all models collapse onto a low-information representation, indicating that today's models remain limited by training data and inductive bias and do not yet encode truly universal structure. Our findings establish representational alignment as a quantitative benchmark for foundation-level generality in scientific models. More broadly, our work can track the emergence of universal representations of matter as models scale, and for selecting and distilling models whose learned representations transfer best across modalities, domains of matter, and scientific tasks.

papers.title: Explaining reaction coordinates of alanine dipeptide isomerization obtained from deep neural networks using Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI)
papers.research_question: How can Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) methods explain which collective variables contribute to the reaction coordinates predicted by deep neural networks for alanine dipeptide isomerization?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that XAI methods (LIME and SHAP) can provide local explanations for the contribution of collective variables to reaction coordinates predicted by a deep neural network for alanine dipeptide isomerization, revealing the importance of specific dihedral angles.
papers.conclusion: The proposed AI-aided method combined with XAI provides a practical tool for locally explaining appropriate reaction coordinates from DNN training, especially near the transition state, and is applicable to complex molecular systems.
papers.key_findings:
Deep neural networks can be trained to predict appropriate reaction coordinates for alanine dipeptide isomerization.
Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanation (LIME) and Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) provide local explanations of feature contributions to the predicted reaction coordinates.
Near the transition state, the dihedral angle θ becomes more important than near the stable states, indicating its role in crossing the barrier.
The feature contributions from LIME and SHAP are consistent, justifying LIME's linear model assumption.
The method can identify dominant collective variables consistent with previous committor test analyses.
papers.limitation: Understanding the detailed mechanism for complex molecular systems becomes complicated because of the large numbers of collective variables.
future_direction: Application to solute-solvent systems such as alanine dipeptide in explicit water.
Application to various other solute-solvent systems.
papers.abstract: A method for obtaining appropriate reaction coordinates is required to identify transition states distinguishing the product and reactant in complex molecular systems. Recently, abundant research has been devoted to obtaining reaction coordinates using artificial neural networks from deep learning literature, where many collective variables are typically utilized in the input layer. However, it is difficult to explain the details of which collective variables contribute to the predicted reaction coordinates owing to the complexity of the nonlinear functions in deep neural networks. To overcome this limitation, we used Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) methods of the Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanation (LIME) and the game theory-based framework known as Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). We demonstrated that XAI enables us to obtain the degree of contribution of each collective variable to reaction coordinates that is determined by nonlinear regressions with deep learning for the committor of the alanine dipeptide isomerization in vacuum. In particular, both LIME and SHAP provide important features to the predicted reaction coordinates, which are characterized by appropriate dihedral angles consistent with those previously reported from the committor test analysis. The present study offers an AI-aided framework to explain the appropriate reaction coordinates, which acquires considerable significance when the number of degrees of freedom increases.

papers.title: Probing Graph Representations
papers.research_question: What is encoded in the representations learned by graph-based models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a probing framework to analyze graph representations and shows that transformer-based graph models capture more chemically relevant information compared to message-passing GNNs.
papers.conclusion: Probing is a useful diagnostic tool for understanding and evaluating graph-based models, especially in capturing domain-relevant information.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer-based models capture more chemically relevant information in their representations.
Randomly initialized models can also encode useful features, sometimes on par with pretrained models.
Skip connections help preserve information across layers.
Pairwise probing can isolate the effect of specific properties and show causal relationships.
papers.abstract: Today we have a good theoretical understanding of the representational power of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). For example, their limitations have been characterized in relation to a hierarchy of Weisfeiler-Lehman (WL) isomorphism tests. However, we do not know what is encoded in the learned representations. This is our main question. We answer it using a probing framework to quantify the amount of meaningful information captured in graph representations. Our findings on molecular datasets show the potential of probing for understanding the inductive biases of graph-based models. We compare different families of models and show that transformer-based models capture more chemically relevant information compared to models based on message passing. We also study the effect of different design choices such as skip connections and virtual nodes. We advocate for probing as a useful diagnostic tool for evaluating graph-based models.

papers.title: Neural Networks Trained to Solve Differential Equations Learn General Representations
papers.research_question: How can we measure the generality of neural network layers across a continuously-parametrized set of tasks? What is the generality structure of layers in neural networks trained to solve differential equations?
papers.core_contribution: We develop an efficient method using SVCCA to measure layer generality across continuously-parametrized tasks, and apply it to show that in neural networks trained to solve differential equations, the first layer is general and deeper layers are successively more specific.
papers.conclusion: We presented a method for measuring layer generality using SVCCA, found that first layers of DENNs are general and deeper layers are more specific, validated with transfer learning, and visualized the general components as generalized coordinates.
papers.key_findings:
The first hidden layer is general, and deeper layers become progressively more specific.
The SVCCA-based method agrees with transfer learning experiments but is much faster, especially for continuously-parametrized problems.
The general components of the first layer can be visualized as generalized coordinates that capture regions of interest in the input domain.
Network width affects layer generality: intrinsic dimensionality saturates with width, reproducibility increases with width, and specificity varies with width and layer depth.
Very wide networks may have training dynamics that affect convergence and generality measurements.
papers.limitation:
SVCCA is numerically unstable when correlation values are very close to each other, making component sorting ill-conditioned.
Very wide networks may have broad minima in the loss landscape, causing training to terminate before optimal convergence, potentially affecting generality measurements.
future_direction: Explore the behavior of layer generality at very large network widths.
Develop component analyses that search for closely-coupled components to improve numerical stability.
Investigate different training protocols for very wide DENNs to ensure proper convergence.
papers.abstract: We introduce a technique based on the singular vector canonical correlation analysis (SVCCA) for measuring the generality of neural network layers across a continuously-parametrized set of tasks. We illustrate this method by studying generality in neural networks trained to solve parametrized boundary value problems based on the Poisson partial differential equation. We find that the first hidden layer is general, and that deeper layers are successively more specific. Next, we validate our method against an existing technique that measures layer generality using transfer learning experiments. We find excellent agreement between the two methods, and note that our method is much faster, particularly for continuously-parametrized problems. Finally, we visualize the general representations of the first layers, and interpret them as generalized coordinates over the input domain.

papers.title: What can attribution methods show us about chemical language models?
papers.research_question: How can attribution methods be used to explain the predictions of a chemical language model for aqueous solubility?
papers.core_contribution: The adapted transformer-specific attribution method produces sparse attributions that reflect how the model maps molecular strings to its latent space, while SHAP provides sensible atom-level attributions but fails to explain functional groups relevant to solubility.
papers.conclusion: Attribution methods provide insight into how chemical language models represent molecules, but current techniques have limitations in explaining solubility predictions in terms of functional groups, instead revealing how the model organizes its latent space.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning the MegaMolBART encoder significantly improves aqueous solubility prediction accuracy.
The transformer-specific attribution method (using the hRi token) yields sparse attributions that are characteristic of how the model represents molecular similarity in its latent space.
SHAP provides chemically sensible attributions (e.g., highlighting electronegative atoms) but does not explain predictions at the level of functional groups.
The fine-tuned model's latent space becomes linearly separable with respect to solubility along the first principal component.
The transformer-specific attribution method cannot propagate negative gradient information, limiting its ability to attribute negative contributions to solubility.
papers.limitation:
The transformer-specific attribution method cannot propagate negative gradient information, preventing attribution of features that negatively contribute to solubility.
SHAP does not capture functional group-level explanations for solubility predictions.
ECFP-based models are less predictive and their explanations are coarse-grained.
future_direction: Using the attributions to design focused, informative chemical datasets by creating training examples that contravene the model's predictions.
papers.abstract: Language models trained on molecular string representations have shown strong performance in predictive and generative tasks. However, practical applications require not only making accurate predictions, but also explainability - the ability to explain the reasons and rationale behind the predictions. In this work, we explore explainability for a chemical language model by adapting a transformer-specific and a model-agnostic input attribution technique. We fine-tune a pretrained model to predict aqueous solubility, compare training and architecture variants, and evaluate visualizations of attributed relevance. The model-agnostic SHAP technique provides sensible attributions, highlighting the positive influence of individual electronegative atoms, but does not explain the model in terms of functional groups or explain how the model represents molecular strings internally to make predictions. In contrast, the adapted transformer-specific explainability technique produces sparse attributions, which cannot be directly attributed to functional groups relevant to solubility. Instead, the attributions are more characteristic of how the model maps molecular strings to its latent space, which seems to represent features relevant to molecular similarity rather than functional groups. These findings provide insight into the representations underpinning chemical language models, which we propose may be leveraged for the design of informative chemical spaces for training more accurate, advanced and explainable models.

papers.title: Peering inside the black box by learning the relevance of many-body functions in neural network potentials
papers.research_question: How can neural network potentials (NNPs), specifically coarse-grained potentials based on graph neural networks, be interpreted by decomposing their inferred energy into n-body interactions to provide human-understandable explanations without compromising predictive power?
papers.core_contribution: This paper extends GNN-LRP (Layer-wise Relevance Propagation for Graph Neural Networks) to interpret neural network potentials for coarse-grained molecular systems, demonstrating that the decomposed n-body interactions are physically meaningful and consistent across different GNN architectures, thereby enhancing trust in these models.
papers.conclusion: The proposed GNN-LRP method successfully interprets neural network potentials by revealing physically sound many-body interactions, providing a strong argument for trusting and wider adoption of these seemingly black-box models in molecular simulations.
papers.key_findings:
GNN-LRP can decompose the energy output of a neural network potential into interpretable n-body (e.g., 2-body and 3-body) interaction contributions.
For coarse-grained methane, 3-body interactions are negligible, while for water they are significant, aligning with fundamental physical knowledge.
Different GNN architectures (PaiNN and SO3Net) trained on the same data learn similar underlying physical interactions, as revealed by their relevance attributions.
GNN-LRP can uncover subtle model artifacts in learned interactions that are not detectable through standard molecular dynamics simulation metrics.
Applied to a coarse-grained protein model (NTL9), GNN-LRP identifies stabilizing and destabilizing residue interactions in different metastable states and correctly interprets the effects of mutations.
papers.limitation: Future work is needed to refine these concepts to provide greater insight into ML models and allow researchers to be more systematic in their choice of architecture and functionalization.
future_direction: Apply the interpretation techniques to extract new scientific knowledge on previously unknown systems.
Refine the GNN-LRP concepts to provide greater insight and allow more systematic choices of architecture and functionalization.
papers.abstract: Machine learned potentials based on artificial neural networks are becoming a popular tool to define an effective energy model for complex systems, either incorporating electronic structure effects at the atomistic resolution, or effectively renormalizing part of the atomistic degrees of freedom at a coarse-grained resolution. One main criticism regarding neural network potentials is that their inferred energy is less interpretable than in traditional approaches, which use simpler and more transparent functional forms. Here we address this problem by extending tools recently proposed in the nascent field of explainable artificial intelligence to coarse-grained potentials based on graph neural networks. With these tools, neural network potentials can be practically decomposed into n-body interactions, providing a human understandable interpretation without compromising predictive power. We demonstrate the approach on three different coarse-grained systems including two fluids (methane and water) and the protein NTL9. The obtained interpretations suggest that well-trained neural network potentials learn physical interactions, which are consistent with fundamental principles.

papers.title: Neural Basis Models for Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we scale Generalized Additive Models (GAMs) to large datasets while maintaining interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Neural Basis Models (NBM), a new subfamily of Generalized Additive Models that uses basis decomposition of shape functions to achieve scalability and interpretability on large datasets.
papers.conclusion: Neural Basis Models address scalability and performance issues of GAMs while preserving interpretability, and can be used as drop-in replacements for black-box deep neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
NBMs achieve state-of-the-art performance among GAMs, with 5x-50x fewer parameters and 4x-7x higher throughput than Neural Additive Models (NAM).
NBMs scale to high-dimensional sparse datasets where other GAMs fail, and are more stable in terms of shape function consistency across training runs.
Pairwise interactions via NB2M can match or exceed the performance of black-box models like MLPs on many datasets.
NBMs can be extended to model pairwise interactions with linear parameter growth, unlike quadratic growth in NA2Ms.
The number of basis functions needed is small (B=100 for NBM, B=200 for NB2M) and the model is not overly sensitive to this choice.
papers.limitation: The approach has limitations with respect to the number of features; beyond 10,000 dense or 1 million sparse features, feature selection is needed to scale further.
future_direction: Explore visual interpretability by applying NBMs directly to pixel space or learning visual features with lower order interactions.
Use more interpretable basis functions, such as polynomials, for higher order interactions.
Apply feature selection algorithms to scale to even larger numbers of features.
papers.abstract: Due to the widespread use of complex machine learning models in real-world applications, it is becoming critical to explain model predictions. However, these models are typically black-box deep neural networks, explained post-hoc via methods with known faithfulness limitations. Generalized Additive Models (GAMs) are an inherently interpretable class of models that address this limitation by learning a non-linear shape function for each feature separately, followed by a linear model on top. However, these models are typically difficult to train, require numerous parameters, and are difficult to scale. We propose an entirely new subfamily of GAMs that utilizes basis decomposition of shape functions. A small number of basis functions are shared among all features, and are learned jointly for a given task, thus making our model scale much better to large-scale data with high-dimensional features, especially when features are sparse. We propose an architecture denoted as the Neural Basis Model (NBM) which uses a single neural network to learn these bases. On a variety of tabular and image datasets, we demonstrate that for interpretable machine learning, NBMs are the state-of-the-art in accuracy, model size, and, throughput and can easily model all higher-order feature interactions. Source code is available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/nbm-spam.

papers.title: Physics Steering: Causal Control of Cross-Domain Concepts in a Physics Foundation Model
papers.research_question: Whether scientific foundation models learn abstract, domain-general representations of physical phenomena that can be causally manipulated via activation steering.
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that a physics foundation model learns linearly steerable representations of physical concepts (e.g., vorticity, diffusion, temporal progression), and that injecting these directions during inference enables fine-grained causal control over simulation behavior. The concept directions are domain-general and transfer across unrelated physical systems.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability techniques from LLMs can be successfully adapted to scientific foundation models, providing evidence that these models develop abstract, domain-general representations of fundamental physical concepts that are linearly encoded and causally steerable.
papers.key_findings:
Single directions in the model's activation space correspond to specific physical concepts like vorticity, diffusion, and simulation speed.
Injecting (adding or subtracting) these concept directions during inference causally steers model predictions, allowing induction or suppression of vortices, enhancement or suppression of diffusion, and speeding up or slowing down simulations.
The extracted concept directions transfer successfully between unrelated physical systems (e.g., from fluid dynamics to chemical reaction-diffusion), indicating they represent abstract, domain-general physical principles.
The results support the Linear Representation Hypothesis for scientific foundation models, showing physical concepts are represented linearly in activation space.
Steering effects are more physically plausible and interpretable when using spatially-averaged concept directions that discard spatial structure, compared to using full spatial tensors.
papers.limitation:
The physical plausibility of the steered results is an open question; including spatial dimensions in the steering tensor can lead to less physically realistic outcomes.
The effectiveness of steering depends on the initial conditions of the simulation; steering becomes more difficult and can produce distorted fields when the initial state is far from the target regime.
future_direction: Exploring the layer-dependence of concept representations and steering effects.
Further work to definitively assess the physicality and self-consistency of steered simulation results.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in mechanistic interpretability have revealed that large language models (LLMs) develop internal representations corresponding not only to concrete entities but also distinct, human-understandable abstract concepts and behaviour. Moreover, these hidden features can be directly manipulated to steer model behaviour. However, it remains an open question whether this phenomenon is unique to models trained on inherently structured data (ie. language, images) or if it is a general property of foundation models. In this work, we investigate the internal representations of a large physics-focused foundation model. Inspired by recent work identifying single directions in activation space for complex behaviours in LLMs, we extract activation vectors from the model during forward passes over simulation datasets for different physical regimes. We then compute "delta" representations between the two regimes. These delta tensors act as concept directions in activation space, encoding specific physical features. By injecting these concept directions back into the model during inference, we can steer its predictions, demonstrating causal control over physical behaviours, such as inducing or removing some particular physical feature from a simulation. These results suggest that scientific foundation models learn generalised representations of physical principles. They do not merely rely on superficial correlations and patterns in the simulations. Our findings open new avenues for understanding and controlling scientific foundation models and has implications for AI-enabled scientific discovery.

papers.title: Comparing the latent features of universal machine-learning interatomic potentials
papers.research_question: How do different universal machine-learning interatomic potentials (uMLIPs) encode chemical information in their latent features, and how do these encodings compare across models, training datasets, and training strategies?
papers.core_contribution: This paper systematically analyzes the latent features of universal machine-learning interatomic potentials (uMLIPs) using feature reconstruction errors, revealing that different models encode chemical information in distinct ways and that these differences can be quantified.
papers.conclusion: Predictive accuracy alone is insufficient to characterize atomistic ML models; feature reconstruction error metrics provide a principled foundation for more transparent, interpretable, and robust model design.
papers.key_findings:
uMLIPs encode the chemical space in significantly distinct ways, with substantial cross-model feature reconstruction errors.
When variants of the same model architecture are considered, trends become dependent on the dataset, target, and training protocol.
Fine-tuning of a uMLIP retains a strong pre-training bias in the latent features.
Atom-level features can be compressed into global structure-level features via concatenation of progressive cumulants, each adding significantly new information.
Backbone features contain more information than last-layer features and are more consistent across models.
papers.abstract: The past few years have seen the development of ``universal'' machine-learning interatomic potentials (uMLIPs) capable of approximating the ground-state potential energy surface across a wide range of chemical structures and compositions with reasonable accuracy. While these models differ in the architecture and the dataset used, they share the ability to compress a staggering amount of chemical information into descriptive latent features. Herein, we systematically analyze what the different uMLIPs have learned by quantitatively assessing the relative information content of their latent features with feature reconstruction errors, and observing how the trends are affected by the choice of training set and training protocol. We find that uMLIPs encode the chemical space in significantly distinct ways, with substantial cross-model feature reconstruction errors. When variants of the same model architecture are considered, trends become dependent on the dataset, target, and training protocol of choice. We also observe that fine-tuning of a uMLIP retains a strong pre-training bias in the latent features. Finally, we discuss how atom-level features, which are directly output by MLIPs, can be compressed into global structure-level features via concatenation of progressive cumulants, each adding significantly new information about the variability across the atomic environments within a given system.

papers.title: Beyond performance: How design choices shape chemical language models
papers.research_question: How do design choices (molecular representation format, tokenization strategy, model architecture) influence the performance and chemical interpretability of chemical language models?
papers.core_contribution: Design choices, particularly molecular representation and tokenization, significantly affect the chemical interpretability of language models, with SMILES and atomwise tokenization yielding more chemically meaningful embeddings, even when downstream task performance is similar.
papers.conclusion: Design choices meaningfully shape how chemical information is represented in language models, and SMILES with atomwise tokenization is favorable for interpretability, guiding future development of chemically grounded CLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Atomwise tokenization generally yields better downstream performance than SentencePiece tokenization.
SMILES representations produce more chemically structured latent spaces than SELFIES representations.
BART and RoBERTa architectures yield comparably interpretable representations, but BART embeddings are more linearly separable for certain molecular properties.
RoBERTa shows a stronger ability to distinguish between atom types than BART.
The choice of molecular representation has a greater impact on interpretability than the model architecture.
future_direction: Exploring alternative molecular representations such as t-SMILES and DeepSMILES.
Comparing BART's generative capabilities with other large language model architectures like GPT.
Investigating the differences and synergies between large language models and graph-based approaches such as GROVER.
Utilizing highly curated datasets from specialized domains to reveal subtle chemical relationships.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Chemical language models (CLMs) have shown strong performance in molecular property prediction and generation tasks. However, the impact of design choices, such as molecular representation format, tokenization strategy, and model architecture, on both performance and chemical interpretability remains underexplored. In this study, we systematically evaluate how these factors influence CLM performance and chemical understanding. We evaluated models through fine-tuning on downstream tasks and probing the structure of their latent spaces using simple classifiers and dimensionality reduction techniques.Despite similar performance on downstream tasks across model configurations, we observed substantial differences in the structure and interpretability of their internal representations. SMILES molecular representation format with atomwise tokenization strategy consistently produced more chemically meaningful embeddings, while models based on BART and RoBERTa architectures yielded comparably interpretable representations. These findings highlight that design choices meaningfully shape how chemical information is represented, even when external metrics appear unchanged. This insight can inform future model development, encouraging more chemically grounded and interpretable CLMs.

papers.title: Analyzing Atomic Interactions in Molecules as Learned by Neural Networks
papers.research_question: To what extent do machine learning force fields (MLFFs) such as SchNet and PaiNN learn underlying physicochemical concepts from data, and how well do their predictions align with known chemical principles?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops an explainable AI (XAI) framework based on GNN-LRP to analyze atomic interactions in machine learning force fields, and finds that models deviating from fundamental chemical principles produce unstable molecular dynamics trajectories despite high prediction accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The proposed XAI framework provides a way to understand and improve machine learning force fields by assessing their adherence to chemical principles, which is crucial for generating stable and physically meaningful simulations.
papers.key_findings:
Interaction strength is atom-type and property dependent.
Intensive properties (e.g., HOMO energy) have a larger interaction range than extensive properties (e.g., atomization energy).
The decay of interaction strength with distance does not follow a polynomial power law as expected from physical principles.
Models exhibit many-body interactions, meaning interaction strength between two atoms depends on the chemical neighborhood.
Models that deviate too far from chemical principles, even with low test errors, produce unstable molecular dynamics simulations.
papers.limitation: The analysis is specific to graph neural networks with a cutoff distance, and the framework's computational complexity is high for large numbers of layers, though approximations mitigate this.
future_direction: Improving ML architectures to better account for the polynomial decay of atomic interactions.
Extending the analysis to other model architectures and a wider range of molecular properties.
papers.abstract: While machine learning (ML) models have been able to achieve unprecedented accuracies across various prediction tasks in quantum chemistry, it is now apparent that accuracy on a test set alone is not a guarantee for robust chemical modeling such as stable molecular dynamics (MD). To go beyond accuracy, we use explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) techniques to develop a general analysis framework for atomic interactions and apply it to the SchNet and PaiNN neural network models. We compare these interactions with a set of fundamental chemical principles to understand how well the models have learned the underlying physicochemical concepts from the data. We focus on the strength of the interactions for different atomic species, how predictions for intensive and extensive quantum molecular properties are made, and analyze the decay and many-body nature of the interactions with interatomic distance. Models that deviate too far from known physical principles produce unstable MD trajectories, even when they have very high energy and force prediction accuracy. We also suggest further improvements to the ML architectures to better account for the polynomial decay of atomic interactions.

papers.title: Interpretability Beyond Feature Attribution: Quantitative Testing with\n Concept Activation Vectors (TCAV)
papers.research_question: How can we interpret neural networks using human-defined concepts and quantify the sensitivity of predictions to these concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs) to represent human-friendly concepts in a model's activation space, and a method (TCAV) to quantify the importance of these concepts to model predictions using directional derivatives.
papers.conclusion: TCAV provides a human-friendly linear interpretation of neural networks, allowing analysts to quantify the importance of user-defined concepts to model predictions, and has been shown to be a useful technique in various applications including bias detection and medical image analysis.
papers.key_findings:
CAVs align with intended concepts, validated by sorting images and activation maximization (deep dream).
TCAV can reveal biases in models, such as gender and race biases in image classifiers.
TCAV quantifies the importance of specific concepts to model classes (e.g., stripes for zebras, red for fire engines).
TCAV can help interpret model errors in medical applications, such as diabetic retinopathy grading.
In a controlled experiment, TCAV more accurately communicated concept importance to humans compared to saliency maps.
future_direction: Applying TCAV to other types of data (audio, video, sequences).
Using TCAV to identify adversarial examples.
Automatically identifying concepts.
papers.abstract:
The interpretation of deep learning models is a challenge due to their size,
complexity, and often opaque internal state. In addition, many systems, such as
image classifiers, operate on low-level features rather than high-level
concepts. To address these challenges, we introduce Concept Activation Vectors
(CAVs), which provide an interpretation of a neural net's internal state in
terms of human-friendly concepts. The key idea is to view the high-dimensional
internal state of a neural net as an aid, not an obstacle. We show how to use
CAVs as part of a technique, Testing with CAVs (TCAV), that uses directional
derivatives to quantify the degree to which a user-defined concept is important
to a classification result--for example, how sensitive a prediction of "zebra"
is to the presence of stripes. Using the domain of image classification as a
testing ground, we describe how CAVs may be used to explore hypotheses and
generate insights for a standard image classification network as well as a
medical application.

papers.title: BERTology Meets Biology: Interpreting Attention in Protein Language Models
papers.research_question: What does attention in protein Transformer language models capture about protein structure and function?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that attention in protein language models captures high-level structural and functional properties of proteins, and that attention focuses on progressively more complex properties with increasing layer depth.
papers.conclusion: Attention in protein Transformer models recovers structural and functional properties of proteins, and interpretability methods can aid scientific discovery.
papers.key_findings:
Attention in deep layers aligns with contact maps, connecting amino acids that are spatially close in 3D structure but far in sequence.
Attention targets binding sites and post-translational modifications, key functional components.
Attention heads specialize in particular amino acids and their patterns are consistent with substitution matrices.
Deeper layers focus more on high-level properties (binding sites, contacts) while secondary structure is targeted more evenly across layers.
Knowledge in embeddings accumulates gradually over layers, while attention acquires knowledge primarily in final layers.
papers.limitation: The analyses are associative and do not establish causal links between attention and model behavior.
future_direction: Using attention and learned representations as tools for scientific discovery.
Developing contextual visualizations of learned representations for domain experts in scientific domains.
papers.abstract: Abstract Transformer architectures have proven to learn useful representations for protein classification and generation tasks. However, these representations present challenges in interpretability. Through the lens of attention, we analyze the inner workings of the Transformer and explore how the model discerns structural and functional properties of proteins. We show that attention (1) captures the folding structure of proteins, connecting amino acids that are far apart in the underlying sequence, but spatially close in the three-dimensional structure, (2) targets binding sites, a key functional component of proteins, and (3) focuses on progressively more complex biophysical properties with increasing layer depth. We also present a three-dimensional visualization of the interaction between attention and protein structure. Our findings align with known biological processes and provide a tool to aid discovery in protein engineering and synthetic biology. The code for visualization and analysis is available at https://github.com/salesforce/provis .

papers.title: The geometry of hidden representations of large transformer models
papers.research_question: How do the geometric and statistical properties of hidden representations evolve across layers in large transformer models, and can the intrinsic dimension profile be used to identify layers with maximal semantic content?
papers.core_contribution: The intrinsic dimension profile of hidden representations in large transformers has a characteristic shape (peak, plateau, etc.), and the layers with minimal intrinsic dimension correspond to those with maximal semantic content, providing an unsupervised strategy to identify optimal layers for downstream tasks.
papers.conclusion: Large transformers behave like sophisticated autoencoders, with an encoding phase (expansion and compression) and a decoding phase, and the low-ID representations in the intermediate layers are semantically rich.
papers.key_findings:
Representations evolve in distinct phases: an initial expansion (high ID), a compression phase (low ID), and a decoding phase.
The ID profile shows a peak in early layers, a plateau/low-ID region in intermediate layers, and sometimes a second peak in later layers.
Semantic information (e.g., protein remote homology, image class labels) is best encoded in the low-ID regions.
The ID profile can be used in an unsupervised manner to identify layers optimal for downstream learning tasks.
The geometric evolution is consistent across transformers trained on different data modalities (protein sequences and images).
papers.limitation:
The use of average pooling to handle variable-length sequences may affect the intrinsic dimension estimates.
Differences in ID profiles between models may be attributed to data modality, training objectives, and preprocessing choices.
The analysis of NLP representations is preliminary and not as extensive as for protein and image models.
future_direction: Analyzing the similarity of representations in ID minima with those from models trained in a supervised setting.
Further investigation of the second peak in iGPT models and its relation to the decoding phase.
Extending the geometric analysis to a broader range of NLP tasks and models.
papers.abstract: Large transformers are powerful architectures used for self-supervised data analysis across various data types, including protein sequences, images, and text. In these models, the semantic structure of the dataset emerges from a sequence of transformations between one representation and the next. We characterize the geometric and statistical properties of these representations and how they change as we move through the layers. By analyzing the intrinsic dimension (ID) and neighbor composition, we find that the representations evolve similarly in transformers trained on protein language tasks and image reconstruction tasks. In the first layers, the data manifold expands, becoming high-dimensional, and then contracts significantly in the intermediate layers. In the last part of the model, the ID remains approximately constant or forms a second shallow peak. We show that the semantic information of the dataset is better expressed at the end of the first peak, and this phenomenon can be observed across many models trained on diverse datasets. Based on our findings, we point out an explicit strategy to identify, without supervision, the layers that maximize semantic content: representations at intermediate layers corresponding to a relative minimum of the ID profile are more suitable for downstream learning tasks.

papers.title: Site-Net: Using global self-attention and real-space supercells to capture long-range interactions in crystal structures
papers.research_question: How can global self-attention and real-space supercells be used to capture long-range interactions in crystal structures for property prediction?
papers.core_contribution: Site-Net is a transformer architecture that uses global self-attention and real-space supercells to capture long-range interactions in crystal structures, achieving state-of-the-art performance on band gap prediction.
papers.conclusion: Site-Net effectively captures long-range interactions in crystal structures and achieves competitive performance on band gap prediction, with potential for improvement via more extensive hyperparameter tuning and the use of larger supercells.
papers.key_findings:
Site-Net achieves a mean absolute error of 0.251 eV on the Matbench band gap regression task, demonstrating competitive performance.
Attention heads in Site-Net become specialized to deal with primarily short- or long-range interactions.
Enforcing a distance cutoff limit of 5 Å on the attention decreases model performance, confirming that longer-range interactions meaningfully contribute to predictions.
Site-Net learns from interactions beyond the nearest neighbor atomic sites.
The model performance is consistent across band gap values.
papers.limitation:
The model is computationally intensive and has a quadratic dependence on the number of atoms in the crystal in terms of VRAM and computational load.
The hyperparameter search was only preliminary, and the hyperparameters used are likely far from optimal.
The cutoff limit of 100 atoms excludes about 3% of crystal structures in the dataset during training due to memory constraints.
Model performance may be limited by the size of the supercell and could improve with larger supercells.
future_direction: More extensive hyperparameter tuning.
Using larger supercells to improve performance.
Applying the method to disordered crystal structures.
papers.abstract: Site-Net is a transformer architecture that models the periodic crystal structures of inorganic materials as a labelled point set of atoms and relies entirely on global self-attention and geometric information to guide learning. Site-Net processes standard crystallographic information files to generate a large real-space supercell, and the importance of interactions between all atomic sites is flexibly learned by the model for the prediction task presented. The attention mechanism is probed to reveal Site-Net can learn long-range interactions in crystal structures, and that specific attention heads become specialized to deal with primarily short- or long-range interactions. We perform a preliminary hyperparameter search and train Site-Net using a single graphics processing unit (GPU), and show Site-Net achieves state-of-the-art performance on a standard band gap regression task.

papers.title: Unveiling Latent Knowledge in Chemistry Language Models through Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How do chemistry language models internally represent chemical knowledge, and can sparse autoencoders uncover interpretable features within these models?
papers.core_contribution: This work presents the first application of sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to chemistry language models, revealing that these models encode a rich hierarchy of interpretable chemical features spanning structural motifs, physicochemical properties, and functional concepts.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders can decompose the latent representations of a chemistry language model into an interpretable feature basis, revealing a rich landscape of chemically meaningful concepts and enabling causal manipulation of molecular structures.
papers.key_findings:
SAE features outperform individual neurons in detecting chemical substructures, especially rare ones, indicating a more disentangled representation.
SAE features provide a compact and decorrelated basis for aligning internal representations with external physicochemical descriptors.
Individual SAE features can capture higher-level functional concepts, such as grouping molecules by shared pharmacological activity (e.g., opioid receptor binding).
Feature steering via ablation demonstrates a causal link between specific features and the generation of corresponding chemical substructures or properties.
The SAE decomposition is information-preserving for downstream tasks (e.g., toxicity prediction) while isolating relevant signals into a more compact set of features than the original neuron basis.
papers.limitation:
The interpretation of features remains a presently unscaled process.
The analysis is confined to a single model architecture (SMI-TED).
The features discovered are contingent on the training data's chemical space, and their generalisation to out-of-distribution molecules remains an open question.
While features are compared to the raw neuron basis, more robust baselines are needed to fully validate the decomposition's effectiveness.
future_direction: Developing methods for the automated interpretation of chemical features.
Exploring applications in AI safety, such as identifying and ablating features correlated with undesirable properties (e.g., toxicity).
Investigating how features behave across different model architectures and scales, including exploring concepts like feature splitting.
papers.abstract: Since the advent of machine learning, interpretability has remained a persistent challenge, becoming increasingly urgent as generative models support high-stakes applications in drug and material discovery. Recent advances in large language model (LLM) architectures have yielded chemistry language models (CLMs) with impressive capabilities in molecular property prediction and molecular generation. However, how these models internally represent chemical knowledge remains poorly understood. In this work, we extend sparse autoencoder techniques to uncover and examine interpretable features within CLMs. Applying our methodology to the Foundation Models for Materials (FM4M) SMI-TED chemistry foundation model, we extract semantically meaningful latent features and analyse their activation patterns across diverse molecular datasets. Our findings reveal that these models encode a rich landscape of chemical concepts. We identify correlations between specific latent features and distinct domains of chemical knowledge, including structural motifs, physicochemical properties, and pharmacological drug classes. Our approach provides a generalisable framework for uncovering latent knowledge in chemistry-focused AI systems. This work has implications for both foundational understanding and practical deployment; with the potential to accelerate computational chemistry research.

papers.title: Phase transition encoded in neural network
papers.research_question: How do temperature-supervised neural networks capture information of phase transition and what physical quantities do they learn?
papers.core_contribution: Temperature-supervised neural networks encode phase transition information in their weights, learning either magnetization or internal energy as features depending on network architecture and prediction accuracy.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks trained to predict temperature encode phase transition information in their weights, and the extracted physical quantity (magnetization or energy) depends on the network architecture and training accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
The fully-connected neural network learns magnetization from input spin configurations, and its weights show a drastic change at the critical temperature, enabling phase transition detection.
The convolutional neural network learns internal energy, achieves higher temperature prediction accuracy, and its weights are proportional to free energy, encoding phase transition information more implicitly.
The phase transition information is captured in the neural network weights even without explicit supervision of phase labels.
The accuracy of temperature prediction is theoretically bounded by the overlap of energy probability distributions at different temperatures.
Convolutional networks perform better because they capture spatial correlations, leading to learning internal energy rather than magnetization.
papers.limitation:
The method may not correctly detect phase transitions driven by different physical mechanisms such as Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) transitions or topological phase transitions.
The fully-connected network only distinguishes between ordered and disordered phases and cannot predict fine-grained temperatures within each phase.
The accuracy of temperature prediction is limited by the overlap of energy distributions at different temperatures in finite systems.
papers.abstract: Abstract We discuss an aspect of neural networks for the purpose of phase transition detection. To this end, we first train the neural network by feeding Ising/Potts configurations with labels of temperature so that it can predict the temperature of the input. We do not explicitly supervise whether the configurations are in the ordered/disordered phase. Nevertheless, we can identify the critical temperature from the parameters (weights and biases) of the trained neural network. We attempt to understand how temperature-supervised neural networks capture information on the phase transition by paying attention to what quantities they learn. Our detailed analyses reveal that they learn different physical quantities depending on how well they are trained. The main observation in this study is how the weights in the trained neural network can have information on the phase transition in addition to temperature.

papers.title: Using attribution to decode binding mechanism in neural network models for chemistry
papers.research_question: Why do virtual screening models make the predictions they do? The paper aims to assess the influence of dataset biases on the prediction of protein binding.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework that uses attribution methods (Integrated Gradients) to test hypotheses about binding logic and reveal dataset bias in neural network models for chemistry, showing that models can achieve perfect accuracy while learning spurious correlations.
papers.conclusion: Attribution methods can reveal dataset bias in neural network models for chemistry, and models can be fooled by adversarial examples despite perfect accuracy. Practitioners should analyze model predictions and not rely solely on aggregate accuracy metrics.
papers.key_findings:
Models trained on synthetic binding logics achieve perfect accuracy on held-out test sets but often have low attribution-AUC, indicating they learn spurious correlations.
Attribution methods (Integrated Gradients) can be used to identify dataset biases and construct adversarial examples that fool the model.
The attribution-AUC metric quantifies how well the model's attributions align with the hypothesized binding logic.
In the ADRB2 dataset, the model achieves perfect accuracy but very low attribution-AUC, indicating it does not learn the correct binding logic.
The framework provides a test for dataset bias given a hypothesis, indicating when models must be simplified/regularized or datasets augmented.
papers.limitation: Attributions offer a reductive view of the model's internal logic and fail to capture higher-order feature interactions.
future_direction: Further research to reveal feature interactions in the model's predictions.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks have achieved state-of-the-art accuracy at classifying molecules with respect to whether they bind to specific protein targets. A key breakthrough would occur if these models could reveal the fragment pharmacophores that are causally involved in binding. Extracting chemical details of binding from the networks could enable scientific discoveries about the mechanisms of drug actions. However, doing so requires shining light into the black box that is the trained neural network model, a task that has proved difficult across many domains. Here we show how the binding mechanism learned by deep neural network models can be interrogated, using a recently described attribution method. We first work with carefully constructed synthetic datasets, in which the molecular features responsible for "binding" are fully known. We find that networks that achieve perfect accuracy on held-out test datasets still learn spurious correlations, and we are able to exploit this nonrobustness to construct adversarial examples that fool the model. This makes these models unreliable for accurately revealing information about the mechanisms of protein-ligand binding. In light of our findings, we prescribe a test that checks whether a hypothesized mechanism can be learned. If the test fails, it indicates that the model must be simplified or regularized and/or that the training dataset requires augmentation.

papers.title: Mechanistic Neural Networks for Scientific Machine Learning
papers.research_question: How can we design neural networks that explicitly learn and solve ordinary differential equations (ODEs) as representations in a parallel and scalable way to enhance interpretability and efficiency in scientific machine learning?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces Mechanistic Neural Networks, a novel neural network design that incorporates a Mechanistic Block to explicitly learn governing differential equations as representations, and a parallel, differentiable ODE solver (NeuRLP) for efficient and scalable training in scientific machine learning.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic Neural Networks are a powerful and versatile approach for scientific machine learning, capable of discovering and modeling complex dynamical systems with high interpretability and efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Mechanistic Neural Networks can discover governing equations from data and outperform the SINDy method in some cases, including for nonlinear and rational function derivatives.
The NeuRLP solver is efficient, parallel, and allows for faster training and longer rollouts compared to traditional sequential ODE solvers like Runge-Kutta.
The method is versatile and achieves competitive or state-of-the-art performance on a range of scientific ML tasks, including PDE solving, equation discovery, and dynamical systems modeling.
The NeuRLP solver can learn adaptive time steps, becoming finer in regions where the fit is poor.
The method can handle multiple independent trajectories and learn a single governing equation from them, improving generalization.
papers.limitation: The cumulative error of the NeuRLP solver can become large for equations where the coefficients c0/c2 and c1/c2 are large relative to the step size.
papers.abstract: This paper presents Mechanistic Neural Networks, a neural network design for machine learning applications in the sciences. It incorporates a new Mechanistic Block in standard architectures to explicitly learn governing differential equations as representations, revealing the underlying dynamics of data and enhancing interpretability and efficiency in data modeling. Central to our approach is a novel Relaxed Linear Programming Solver (NeuRLP) inspired by a technique that reduces solving linear ODEs to solving linear programs. This integrates well with neural networks and surpasses the limitations of traditional ODE solvers enabling scalable GPU parallel processing. Overall, Mechanistic Neural Networks demonstrate their versatility for scientific machine learning applications, adeptly managing tasks from equation discovery to dynamic systems modeling. We prove their comprehensive capabilities in analyzing and interpreting complex scientific data across various applications, showing significant performance against specialized state-of-the-art methods.

papers.title: On the definition and importance of interpretability in scientific machine learning
papers.research_question: What is interpretability in the context of scientific machine learning, and how does interpretability advance scientific knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a definition of interpretability for scientific machine learning that emphasizes understanding of the mechanism over mathematical sparsity, and questions the possibility of interpretable scientific discovery when prior knowledge is lacking.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes by proposing a definition of interpretability focused on physical meaning, and argues that interpretability is useful in science as a tool for unification, with sparsity facilitating derivation from fundamental principles.
papers.key_findings:
Researchers in equation discovery and symbolic regression tend to conflate the concept of sparsity with interpretability.
Existing definitions and methods from the broader interpretable ML literature are inadequate for scientific machine learning.
Interpretability in science should be defined as understanding the physical meaning or mechanism of an equation, not merely its mathematical sparsity.
Sparsity is neither necessary nor sufficient for interpretability in science; prior knowledge is required to connect sparse equations to underlying principles.
Interpretability advances scientific knowledge by unifying disparate phenomena under a small set of fundamental physical principles.
future_direction: Future work will explore whether interpretations can be extracted from recovered equations when relevant prior knowledge is lacking.
papers.abstract: Though neural networks trained on large datasets have been successfully used to describe and predict many physical phenomena, there is a sense among scientists that, unlike traditional scientific models comprising simple mathematical expressions, their findings cannot be integrated into the body of scientific knowledge. Critics of machine learning's inability to produce human-understandable relationships have converged on the concept of "interpretability" as its point of departure from more traditional forms of science. As the growing interest in interpretability has shown, researchers in the physical sciences seek not just predictive models, but also to uncover the fundamental principles that govern a system of interest. However, clarity around a definition of interpretability and the precise role that it plays in science is lacking in the literature. In this work, we argue that researchers in equation discovery and symbolic regression tend to conflate the concept of sparsity with interpretability. We review key papers on interpretable machine learning from outside the scientific community and argue that, though the definitions and methods they propose can inform questions of interpretability for scientific machine learning (SciML), they are inadequate for this new purpose. Noting these deficiencies, we propose an operational definition of interpretability for the physical sciences. Our notion of interpretability emphasizes understanding of the mechanism over mathematical sparsity. Innocuous though it may seem, this emphasis on mechanism shows that sparsity is often unnecessary. It also questions the possibility of interpretable scientific discovery when prior knowledge is lacking. We believe a precise and philosophically informed definition of interpretability in SciML will help focus research efforts toward the most significant obstacles to realizing a data-driven scientific future.

papers.title: Scale-invariant feature extraction of neural network and renormalization group flow
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between the Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM) and renormalization group (RG) flow, and how does the RBM learn to extract features from spin configurations?
papers.core_contribution: The unsupervised RBM trained on Ising model configurations at various temperatures generates a flow of temperature that approaches the critical point Tc, opposite to the typical RG flow, indicating the RBM learns scale-invariant features.
papers.conclusion: The RBM flow is attracted to the critical point when trained on a wide range of temperatures, and the RBM learns scale-invariant features, showing a connection to RG but with an opposite flow direction.
papers.key_findings:
For type V RBM (trained on configurations from T=0 to T=6), the temperature flow approaches the critical temperature Tc=2.27, making Tc a stable fixed point.
When the hidden layer size Nh is less than or equal to the visible layer size Nv, the flow stabilizes at Tc; for Nh > Nv, the flow eventually moves towards high temperature.
The weight matrix product WW^T reflects spin correlations, and its off-diagonal components decay similarly to spin correlations near Tc.
The eigenvalue spectrum of WW^T for type V RBM shows a gradual decrease without jumps, suggesting scale-invariant feature learning.
The RBM flow is attracted to the features it has learned during training, e.g., type H/L RBMs flow towards high/low temperatures respectively.
future_direction: Investigate the RBM flow for first-order phase transitions, e.g., in the Blume-Capel model.
Study the attractor of RBM flows for human faces to understand value judgments.
Describe the RBM flow as a stochastic process using Langevin or Fokker-Planck equations.
papers.abstract: Theoretical understanding of how a deep neural network (DNN) extracts features from input images is still unclear, but it is widely believed that the extraction is performed hierarchically through a process of coarse graining. It reminds us of the basic renormalization group (RG) concept in statistical physics. In order to explore possible relations between DNN and RG, we use the restricted Boltzmann machine (RBM) applied to an Ising model and construct a flow of model parameters (in particular, temperature) generated by the RBM. We show that the unsupervised RBM trained by spin configurations at various temperatures from T=0 to T=6 generates a flow along which the temperature approaches the critical value T_{c}=2.27. This behavior is the opposite of the typical RG flow of the Ising model. By analyzing various properties of the weight matrices of the trained RBM, we discuss why it flows towards T_{c} and how the RBM learns to extract features of spin configurations.

papers.title: Exploiting Latent Linearity in LLMs Improves Explainable Molecular Representation Learning
papers.research_question: Can LLM-derived molecular representations be linearly decomposed into chemically meaningful concepts (functional groups), and how can this latent linearity be exploited for explainable molecular property prediction?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces MoleX, a framework that decomposes LLM latent representations into a concept-aligned space of functional groups and shows that a sparse linear mapping onto these chemical concepts improves both predictive accuracy and explainability for molecular property prediction.
papers.conclusion: Exploiting latent linearity in LLM representations provides a principled basis for effective and explainable molecular representation learning, improving accuracy, explainability, and efficiency in molecular property prediction.
papers.key_findings:
LLM-derived molecular representations exhibit latent linearity that can be expressed as a weighted combination of chemically meaningful functional group concepts.
MoleX outperforms existing GNN, LLM, and explainable machine learning baselines in predictive accuracy and explanation faithfulness on benchmark molecular property prediction tasks.
A residual calibration strategy corrects errors from the base linear predictor, further improving accuracy and explanation alignment with ground-truth substructures.
MoleX achieves significant computational efficiency, with CPU inference over 300x faster than LLMs and using 100,000 fewer parameters.
The linear predictor's performance scales with model size, training precision, and dataset size, but task-adapted training is crucial for converting capacity into performance gains.
papers.limitation: The linear predictor may underfit complex molecular patterns in some cases, as there is a trade-off between model complexity and performance.
future_direction: Examine the complexity–performance trade-off in LLM-based molecular representation learning to identify optimal balances between model complexity and downstream performance.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated broad utility across molecular domains, spanning drug discovery and materials design. Analyzing LLMs' latent representations is crucial for elucidating their underlying mechanisms, improving explainability, and ultimately advancing downstream performance. We propose MoleX, a simple yet effective framework that decomposes molecular embeddings within LLM representations into a concept-aligned space for explainable molecular representation learning. We further show that these high-dimensional embeddings admit a linear mapping onto chemically consistent concepts. Our analysis suggests that the uncovered linearity aligns with established chemical principles, indicating a mechanistically explainable latent structure in LLM representations for scientific applications. When applied to downstream tasks, this latent linearity improves both predictive and explanatory performance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MoleX outperforms existing approaches in accuracy, explainability, and efficiency, achieving CPU inference on large-scale datasets 300 times faster with 100,000 fewer parameters than LLMs.

papers.title: A comparison of explainable artificial intelligence methods in the phase classification of multi-principal element alloys
papers.research_question: How do two model-agnostic local post-hoc interpretability methods (breakDown and SHAP) compare in explaining the predictions of a black-box classification model for multi-principal element alloy phase formation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that both breakDown and SHAP interpretability methods can identify composition clusters with similar phase labels, with SHAP agreeing more closely with literature, and reveals that there can be multiple explanations for phase formation rules in multi-principal element alloys.
papers.conclusion: Both breakDown and SHAP are useful for interpretability in materials science, and there is more than one explanation for phase formation rules in multi-principal element alloys.
papers.key_findings:
Both breakDown and SHAP transformed data capture aggregation of chemical compositions with similar phase labels when visualized with t-SNE.
Variable attribution from breakDown and SHAP do not agree on all levels, but SHAP results are more consistent with published literature.
Despite differences in variable attribution, k-means clustering on breakDown and SHAP data yields similar composition clusters (e.g., 87% overlap for FCC clusters).
CP profile plots show similar functional dependencies between feature values and predicted responses for clusters from both methods.
The ensemble SVM model produces large error bars in variable attribution, indicating model-to-model variation due to limited data.
papers.limitation:
Materials science suffers from limited and sparse data, which affects model training and interpretability.
The eSVM method produces large error bars in variable attribution, suggesting large model-to-model variation between ensembles due to limited samples.
The independence assumption of input features may not hold completely, which affects the breakDown method.
