papers.research_question: How can we quantify the interpretability of latent representations in CNNs by measuring the alignment between individual hidden units and semantic concepts, and what factors affect this interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Network Dissection, a framework for quantifying the interpretability of CNN representations by evaluating the alignment between individual convolutional units and a broad set of semantic concepts, and uses it to show interpretability is an axis-aligned property affected by architecture, training data, and regularization.
papers.conclusion: Network Dissection provides a method to quantify interpretability in CNNs, revealing that interpretability is an axis-aligned property indicative of partially disentangled representations, and is influenced by network architecture, training data, and training techniques.
papers.key_findings:
Interpretability of units is not axis-independent; random rotations of the representation significantly reduce the number of unique concept detectors, indicating interpretability is a special alignment learned by the network.
Deeper network architectures (ResNet > VGG > GoogLeNet > AlexNet) and training on scene-centric data (Places) lead to more interpretable units (more unique concept detectors).
Self-supervised training tasks produce fewer object detectors and more texture detectors compared to supervised training, and the form of self-supervision (e.g., colorization) affects which concepts emerge.
Batch normalization significantly reduces interpretability, while dropout and different random initializations have less impact on the final level of interpretability.
Widening a convolutional layer (increasing the number of units) can increase the number of unique concept detectors without significantly harming classification accuracy.
papers.limitation: Network dissection works only as well as the underlying dataset; if a unit matches a human-understandable concept that is absent in Broden, it will not score well for interpretability.
future_direction: Expanding the Broden dataset to include more kinds of visual concepts.
Finding ways to capture the benefits of batch normalization without destroying interpretability.
papers.abstract: We propose a general framework called Network Dissection for quantifying the interpretability of latent representations of CNNs by evaluating the alignment between individual hidden units and a set of semantic concepts. Given any CNN model, the proposed method draws on a data set of concepts to score the semantics of hidden units at each intermediate convolutional layer. The units with semantics are labeled across a broad range of visual concepts including objects, parts, scenes, textures, materials, and colors. We use the proposed method to test the hypothesis that interpretability is an axis-independent property of the representation space, then we apply the method to compare the latent representations of various networks when trained to solve different classification problems. We further analyze the effect of training iterations, compare networks trained with different initializations, and measure the effect of dropout and batch normalization on the interpretability of deep visual representations. We demonstrate that the proposed method can shed light on characteristics of CNN models and training methods that go beyond measurements of their discriminative power.

papers.title: Collective variables of neural networks: empirical time evolution and scaling laws
papers.research_question: How can the entropy and trace of the empirical neural tangent kernel (NTK) be used to understand learning dynamics and scaling relations in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces entropy and trace of the empirical neural tangent kernel as collective variables to analyze neural network training dynamics, identifying two learning regimes (information compression and structure formation) and showing that structure formation characterizes the deep learning regime.
papers.conclusion: Entropy and trace of the NTK provide a universal framework for understanding neural network learning dynamics and scaling, with structure formation identified as a hallmark of deep learning.
papers.key_findings:
Entropy of the NTK reveals two learning regimes: information compression (entropy decreases) where gradient vectors align, and structure formation (entropy increases) where the network separates data to create richer representations.
Small networks tend to remain in the compression regime with limited performance, while large networks transition to structure formation, which is associated with improved performance and defines a deep learning regime.
The trace of the NTK, representing an effective learning rate, increases during training, indicating growing network sensitivity to new data and potential vulnerabilities to adversarial attacks or benefits for continual learning.
The dynamics observed via entropy and trace are universal across diverse architectures including transformers, GNNs, CNNs, and reinforcement learning agents.
Architecture scaling (width and depth) influences the entropy and trace, with deeper networks showing reduced entropy at initialization but capable of achieving higher entropy after training when sufficiently wide.
future_direction: Explore how scaling behavior for different activation functions can be used for targeted architecture selection.
Investigate the trace property to reduce model sensitivity and improve continual learning strategies.
Explore avenues for improved stability by reducing trace late in training.
papers.abstract: This work presents a novel means for understanding learning dynamics and scaling relations in neural networks. We show that certain measures on the spectrum of the empirical neural tangent kernel, specifically entropy and trace, yield insight into the representations learned by a neural network and how these can be improved through architecture scaling. These results are demonstrated first on test cases before being shown on more complex networks, including transformers, auto-encoders, graph neural networks, and reinforcement learning studies. In testing on a wide range of architectures, we highlight the universal nature of training dynamics and further discuss how it can be used to understand the mechanisms behind learning in neural networks. We identify two such dominant mechanisms present throughout machine learning training. The first, information compression, is seen through a reduction in the entropy of the NTK spectrum during training, and occurs predominantly in small neural networks. The second, coined structure formation, is seen through an increasing entropy and thus, the creation of structure in the neural network representations beyond the prior established by the network at initialization. Due to the ubiquity of the latter in deep neural network architectures and its flexibility in the creation of feature-rich representations, we argue that this form of evolution of the network's entropy be considered the onset of a deep learning regime.

papers.title: Ensuring Medical AI Safety: Interpretability-Driven Detection and Mitigation of Spurious Model Behavior and Associated Data
papers.research_question: How can interpretability methods be used to detect and mitigate spurious correlations (shortcut learning) in deep neural networks for medical AI, and how can bias annotation be semi-automated to reduce manual labeling effort?
papers.core_contribution: The paper extends the Reveal2Revise framework with semi-automated interpretability-based bias annotation capabilities, enabling sample- and feature-level annotation of spurious correlations to reduce manual labeling and improve bias mitigation in medical AI models.
papers.conclusion: The interpretability-driven Reveal2Revise framework, enhanced with bias annotation capabilities, provides a comprehensive approach to improve medical AI safety by detecting and mitigating spurious model behavior, ultimately increasing model robustness for real-world deployment.
papers.key_findings:
The extended Reveal2Revise framework successfully identifies and mitigates both controlled and real-world spurious correlations across four medical datasets and multiple model architectures.
The framework provides sample-level bias annotation via data retrieval using concept representations (e.g., CAVs) and feature-level annotation via spatial localization of artifacts.
Bias mitigation methods like RRR and RR-ClArC, when integrated with the framework, improve model robustness by reducing reliance on spurious features while maintaining accuracy on clean data.
The approach reduces the need for extensive manual annotation by domain experts, making bias detection and mitigation more practical.
The framework is applicable across different modalities (image and ECG) and model types (CNNs and Vision Transformers).
papers.limitation:
The framework requires human validation to distinguish between clinically valid and spurious outlier behavior.
Some artifacts are non-localizable (e.g., brightness shifts), limiting spatial bias localization.
Bias representations (e.g., CAVs) may be inaccurate if the initial set of biased samples is small or noisy.
future_direction: Extending the framework to other modalities and data types.
Improving the automation of bias detection and validation to further reduce human effort.
Integrating the framework with a wider range of bias mitigation techniques.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks are increasingly employed in high-stakes medical applications, despite their tendency for shortcut learning in the presence of spurious correlations, which can have potentially fatal consequences in practice. Whereas a multitude of works address either the detection or mitigation of such shortcut behavior in isolation, the Reveal2Revise approach provides a comprehensive bias mitigation framework combining these steps. However, effectively addressing these biases often requires substantial labeling efforts from domain experts. In this work, we review the steps of the Reveal2Revise framework and enhance it with semi-automated interpretability-based bias annotation capabilities. This includes methods for the sample- and feature-level bias annotation, providing valuable information for bias mitigation methods to unlearn the undesired shortcut behavior. We show the applicability of the framework using four medical datasets across two modalities, featuring controlled and real-world spurious correlations caused by data artifacts. We successfully identify and mitigate these biases in VGG16, ResNet50, and contemporary Vision Transformer models, ultimately increasing their robustness and applicability for real-world medical tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/frederikpahde/medical-ai-safety.

papers.title: Self-Supervised Vision Transformers Learn Visual Concepts in Histopathology
papers.research_question: Can self-supervised learning, particularly DINO-based knowledge distillation, learn data-efficient and interpretable features in histology images?
papers.core_contribution: Vision Transformers using DINO-based self-supervised learning learn data-efficient and interpretable features in histology images, with different attention heads capturing distinct morphological phenotypes.
papers.conclusion: Self-supervised learning, particularly DINO, is effective for learning representations in histopathology, and the attention heads of Vision Transformers provide interpretable visual concepts that can aid in biomarker discovery.
papers.key_findings:
ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50 features are a strong baseline, achieving comparable performance to self-supervised methods on many tasks.
Self-supervised features, particularly from DINO, are robust and sample-efficient, performing well with less training data.
DINO outperforms SimCLR on weakly-supervised and patch-level tasks in histopathology.
DINO's attention heads learn distinct morphological visual concepts, localizing cells, stroma tissue, and fat/air pockets.
papers.limitation: Performance benefit of self-supervised learning may vary depending on organ type (only breast tissue tested) and weakly-supervised architecture (only CLAM tested).
future_direction: Assess the utility of self-supervised methods for learning representations of histopathological images from rare diseases with data paucity of slide-level and patch-level annotations.
papers.abstract: Tissue phenotyping is a fundamental task in learning objective characterizations of histopathologic biomarkers within the tumor-immune microenvironment in cancer pathology. However, whole-slide imaging (WSI) is a complex computer vision in which: 1) WSIs have enormous image resolutions with precludes large-scale pixel-level efforts in data curation, and 2) diversity of morphological phenotypes results in inter- and intra-observer variability in tissue labeling. To address these limitations, current efforts have proposed using pretrained image encoders (transfer learning from ImageNet, self-supervised pretraining) in extracting morphological features from pathology, but have not been extensively validated. In this work, we conduct a search for good representations in pathology by training a variety of self-supervised models with validation on a variety of weakly-supervised and patch-level tasks. Our key finding is in discovering that Vision Transformers using DINO-based knowledge distillation are able to learn data-efficient and interpretable features in histology images wherein the different attention heads learn distinct morphological phenotypes. We make evaluation code and pretrained weights publicly-available at: https://github.com/Richarizardd/Self-Supervised-ViT-Path.

papers.title: Structure and Representation in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we find modular structure in neural networks, and does this structure have functional relevance in terms of local specialization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that trained neural networks exhibit clusterability (modular structure) and that clustering can find locally specialized groups of neurons. It also shows that interpretability tools reveal shortcomings in reward models' feature representation and generalization.
papers.conclusion: The dissertation advances understanding of neural network structure and representation, and highlights the need for better interpretability tools to understand generalization behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Trained neural networks are more clusterable than randomly initialized networks.
Clustering finds groups of neurons that are important and coherent, indicating local specialization.
Interpretability tools applied to reward models show they do not adequately represent relevant features and mispredict reward out of distribution.
These tools do not reveal a clear picture of the computation the networks are performing.
There is a need for better interpretability tools to understand generalization behavior.
papers.limitation: Interpretability tools do not reveal a clear picture of what computation the networks are performing.
future_direction: Applying the methods to larger networks.
Studying the dynamics of clusterability during training.
Developing better interpretability tools for understanding generalization.
papers.abstract: Since neural networks have become dominant within the field of artificial intelligence, a sub-field of research has emerged attempting to understand their inner workings. One standard method within this sub-field has been to primarily understand neural networks as representing human-comprehensible features. Another possibility that has been less explored is to understand them as multi-step computer programs. A seeming prerequisite for this is some form of modularity: for different parts of the network to operate independently enough to be understood in isolation, and to implement distinct interpretable sub-routines.To find modular structure inside neural networks, we initially use the tools of graphical clustering. A network is clusterable in this sense if it can be divided into groups of neurons with strong internal connectivity but weak external connectivity. We find that a trained neural network is typically more clusterable than randomly initialized networks, and often clusterable relative to random networks with the same distribution of weights as the trained network. We investigate factors that promote clusterability, and also develop novel methods targeted at that end.For modularity to be valuable for understanding neural networks, it needs to have some sort of functional relevance.The type of functional relevance we target is local specialization of functionality. A neural network is locally specialized to the extent that parts of its computational graph can be abstractly represented as performing some comprehensible sub-task relevant to the overall task. We propose two proxies for local specialization: importance, which reflects how valuable sets of neurons are to network performance; and coherence, which reflects how consistently their neurons associate with features of the inputs. We then operationalize these proxies using techniques conventionally used to interpret individual neurons, applying them instead to groups of neurons produced by graph clustering algorithms. Our results show that clustering succeeds at finding groups of neurons that are important and coherent, although not all groups of neurons found are so.We conclude with a case study of using more standard interpretability tools, designed to understand the features being represented by directions in activation space, applying them to the analysis of neural networks trained on the reward function of the game CoinRun. Despite our networks achieving a low test loss, the application of interpretability tools shows that networks do not adequately represent relevant features and badly mispredict reward out of distribution. That said, these tools do not reveal a clear picture of what computation the networks are in fact performing. This not only illustrates the need for better interpretability tools to understand generalization behaviour, but motivates it: if we take these networks as models of 'motivation systems' of policies trained by reinforcement learning, the conclusion is that such networks may competently pursue the wrong objectives when deployed in richer environments, indicating a need for interpretability techniques to shed light on generalization behaviour.

papers.title: Manifolds and Modules: How Function Develops in a Neural Foundation Model
papers.research_question: Do neural decoding and encoding manifolds reveal new insights into how foundation models represent temporal response patterns? Are the representations brain-like?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes a neural foundation model (FNN) using decoding/encoding manifolds and trajectories, finding that different processing stages (encoder, recurrent, readout) exhibit distinct representational structures. The recurrent module enriches temporal representations, while the readout achieves biological fidelity through numerous specialized feature maps rather than biologically plausible mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: Neural foundation models may be more similar in internal operation to other foundation models than to their biological counterparts. Future architectures incorporating recurrence after a light-weight retinal-like encoder and constraining feature dimensionality to match biological cell type diversity could bridge the gap between computational performance and biological plausibility.
papers.key_findings:
The feedforward encoder module lacks biologically plausible stimulus-dependent temporal patterns and mainly reports input features with varying intensity.
The recurrent module shows a jump in capabilities by 'pushing apart' representations of different temporal stimulus patterns, enabling better stimulus separability.
The readout module accounts for biological variability by relying on a large number of self-similar feature maps, differing from known biological counterparts in V1.
The output layer achieves a continuous representation by linearly combining the readout features to associate spike trains with input movies.
The model's internal dynamics (quantified by tubularity metrics) are less complex and entangled than those observed in biological retina and V1 data.
papers.limitation:
The analysis utilized a single foundation model, due to the limited availability of other video-based foundation models of neural activity over time.
The work used a restricted set of stimuli to ensure comparability to biological results.
future_direction: Future architectures incorporating recurrence directly after a more light-weight retinal-like encoder.
Constraining feature dimensionality to match biological cell type diversity to yield models that bridge the gap between computational performance and biological plausibility.
papers.abstract: Foundation models have shown remarkable success in fitting biological visual systems; however, their black-box nature inherently limits their utility for understanding brain function. Here, we peek inside a SOTA foundation model of neural activity (Wang et al., 2025) as a physiologist might, characterizing each 'neuron' based on its temporal response properties to parametric stimuli. We analyze how different stimuli are represented in neural activity space by building decoding manifolds, and we analyze how different neurons are represented in stimulus-response space by building neural encoding manifolds. We find that the different processing stages of the model (i.e., the feedforward encoder, recurrent, and readout modules) each exhibit qualitatively different representational structures in these manifolds. The recurrent module shows a jump in capabilities over the encoder module by 'pushing apart' the representations of different temporal stimulus patterns; while the readout module achieves biological fidelity by using numerous specialized feature maps rather than biologically plausible mechanisms. Overall, we present this work as a study of the inner workings of a prominent neural foundation model, gaining insights into the biological relevance of its internals through the novel analysis of its neurons' joint temporal response patterns.

papers.title: Explainable Molecular Property Prediction: Aligning Chemical Concepts with Predictions via Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we provide chemically meaningful and faithful explanations for molecular property predictions using language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Lamole, a framework for explainable molecular property prediction that uses Group SELFIES representation and combines attention weights with gradients, calibrated by a marginal loss, to provide chemically meaningful and faithful explanations.
papers.conclusion: Lamole provides chemically meaningful and faithful explanations for molecular property prediction and can be integrated into an interpretable optimization pipeline for molecular design.
papers.key_findings:
Lamole achieves prediction accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art baselines while improving explanation accuracy by up to 14.3%.
The proposed information flow-based explanation method, integrating attention and gradients, captures interactions between functional groups.
The marginal loss aligns explanations with the tangent space of the data manifold, ensuring concept-aligned results.
Using only 10% of molecules with ground truth annotations can significantly improve explanation accuracy.
Integration with an evolutionary algorithm demonstrates Lamole's actionable utility for guiding molecular editing and optimization.
papers.limitation:
Complex interactions caused by multiple functional groups may not be fully captured, and other functional groups may receive relatively high importance scores.
The molecular editing case is a computational demonstration and does not imply real-world chemical optimality.
future_direction: Extending the framework to broader generalization scenarios, including unseen chemotypes.
Designing more strategies to reveal complex functional group interactions.
papers.abstract: Providing explainable molecular property predictions is critical for many scientific domains, such as drug discovery and material science. Though transformer-based language models have shown great potential in accurate molecular property prediction, they neither provide chemically meaningful explanations nor faithfully reveal the molecular structure-property relationships. In this work, we develop a framework for explainable molecular property prediction based on language models, dubbed as Lamole, which can provide chemical concepts-aligned explanations. We take a string-based molecular representation -- Group SELFIES -- as input tokens to pretrain and fine-tune our Lamole, as it provides chemically meaningful semantics. By disentangling the information flows of Lamole, we propose combining self-attention weights and gradients for better quantification of each chemically meaningful substructure's impact on the model's output. To make the explanations more faithfully respect the structure-property relationship, we then carefully craft a marginal loss to explicitly optimize the explanations to be able to align with the chemists' annotations. We bridge the manifold hypothesis with the elaborated marginal loss to prove that the loss can align the explanations with the tangent space of the data manifold, leading to concept-aligned explanations. Experimental results over six mutagenicity datasets and one hepatotoxicity dataset demonstrate Lamole can achieve comparable classification accuracy and boost the explanation accuracy by up to 14.3%, being the state-of-the-art in explainable molecular property prediction.

papers.title: Interpreting Neural Networks through the Polytope Lens
papers.research_question: What are the fundamental primitives of neural network representations, and can polytopes serve as a better unit of description than neurons or directions?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the polytope lens, a perspective that accounts for nonlinearities in neural networks, and demonstrates that polytopes can identify monosemantic regions and that polytope boundaries correspond to semantic boundaries.
papers.conclusion: The polytope lens provides a more accurate description of neural networks by incorporating nonlinearities, but further work is needed to develop it into a practical tool for mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Polysemantic directions overlap with multiple monosemantic polytope regions.
Polytope boundaries reflect semantic boundaries, with denser boundaries between different classes than within the same class.
Polytopes partially define when feature-directions are on- and off-distribution, with dense boundaries near the origin but class changes also occur in low-density regions.
Clustering activations or spline codes yields monosemantic clusters in both image classifiers and language models.
The polytope lens provides a more complete description of neural networks by incorporating nonlinearities, but it is not yet clear how to use it for decomposable descriptions.
papers.limitation: The polytope lens sacrifices globally valid feature directions for locally valid ones, making descriptions more complex and less decomposable.
future_direction: Develop the polytope lens into a practical tool for mechanistic interpretability.
Build more robust and scalable methods based on the polytope lens.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to explain what a neural network has learned at a nuts-and-bolts level. What are the fundamental primitives of neural network representations? Previous mechanistic descriptions have used individual neurons or their linear combinations to understand the representations a network has learned. But there are clues that neurons and their linear combinations are not the correct fundamental units of description: directions cannot describe how neural networks use nonlinearities to structure their representations. Moreover, many instances of individual neurons and their combinations are polysemantic (i.e. they have multiple unrelated meanings). Polysemanticity makes interpreting the network in terms of neurons or directions challenging since we can no longer assign a specific feature to a neural unit. In order to find a basic unit of description that does not suffer from these problems, we zoom in beyond just directions to study the way that piecewise linear activation functions (such as ReLU) partition the activation space into numerous discrete polytopes. We call this perspective the polytope lens. The polytope lens makes concrete predictions about the behavior of neural networks, which we evaluate through experiments on both convolutional image classifiers and language models. Specifically, we show that polytopes can be used to identify monosemantic regions of activation space (while directions are not in general monosemantic) and that the density of polytope boundaries reflect semantic boundaries. We also outline a vision for what mechanistic interpretability might look like through the polytope lens.

papers.title: Neural network interpretation using descrambler groups
papers.research_question: How can inner layer signalling of fully connected neural networks be brought into a human-readable form to improve interpretability, particularly in digital signal processing and scientific computing?
papers.core_contribution: A group-theoretical method (descrambler groups) for interpreting fully connected neural networks by finding orthogonal transformations that make intermediate signals human-readable, successfully revealing sophisticated signal processing operations in a DSP network.
papers.conclusion: The descrambler group method enables interpretation of fully connected neural networks, revealing that even small networks can invent complex mathematical operations, and that reductionist understanding is possible.
papers.key_findings:
The descrambler group method can successfully interpret the inner workings of fully connected neural networks.
DEERNet spontaneously invents a bandpass filter, a notch filter, a frequency axis rectifier, frequency division multiplexing, spectral filtering regularization, and a Fourier-like transform mapping harmonics to Chebyshev polynomials.
The method reveals that even small networks can develop complex, interpretable mathematical operations during training.
The descrambling process requires defining a problem-specific interpretability metric, such as signal smoothness or diagonal dominance.
The method is applicable to fully connected layers, which are harder to interpret than convolutional layers.
papers.limitation: The method requires domain-specific expertise to recognize the functionality of descrambled weight matrices, and the descrambled matrix may still be uninterpretable to non-specialists.
future_direction: Neural networks can be mined for new knowledge, possibly discovering previously unknown mathematics.
A staged approach is recommended: first establish the role of each layer empirically, then descramble for implementation details.
papers.abstract: The lack of interpretability and trust is a much-criticized feature of deep neural networks. In fully connected nets, the signaling between inner layers is scrambled because backpropagation training does not require perceptrons to be arranged in any particular order. The result is a black box; this problem is particularly severe in scientific computing and digital signal processing (DSP), where neural nets perform abstract mathematical transformations that do not reduce to features or concepts. We present here a group-theoretical procedure that attempts to bring inner-layer signaling into a human-readable form, the assumption being that this form exists and has identifiable and quantifiable features-for example, smoothness or locality. We applied the proposed method to DEERNet (a DSP network used in electron spin resonance) and managed to descramble it. We found considerable internal sophistication: the network spontaneously invents a bandpass filter, a notch filter, a frequency axis rescaling transformation, frequency-division multiplexing, group embedding, spectral filtering regularization, and a map from harmonic functions into Chebyshev polynomials-in 10 min of unattended training from a random initial guess.

papers.title: Interpreting GFlowNets for Drug Discovery: Extracting Actionable Insights for Medicinal Chemistry
papers.research_question: How can interpretability methods be adapted to structured generative models like GFlowNets to provide actionable insights for medicinal chemistry in drug discovery?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an interpretability framework for GFlowNets that reveals how SynFlowNet encodes chemical properties like polarity and lipophilicity, and provides actionable insights for drug discovery through counterfactual saliency and motif analysis.
papers.conclusion: The study extends interpretability tools to GFlowNets, showing that SynFlowNet's internal representations align with chemical intuition, and suggests future directions like multi-objective analysis and direct conditioning on physicochemical properties.
papers.key_findings:
Gradient-based saliency with counterfactual edits identifies atom- and motif-level regions that systematically affect predicted drug-likeness (QED).
Sparse autoencoders applied to SynFlowNet embeddings reveal latent factors that correlate strongly with physicochemical properties such as polarity, lipophilicity, and size.
Motif probes show that functional groups like halogens and aromatic rings are encoded in a linearly decodable manner in the embeddings.
The interpretability framework links model decisions to medicinal chemistry heuristics, enabling actionable insights for molecule design.
The approach demonstrates that GFlowNets can be interpreted using adapted methods from supervised learning, extending interpretability to structured generative policies.
papers.limitation:
Focuses primarily on QED, limiting generalization to multi-objective settings.
Disentanglement methods like sparse autoencoders and motif probes impose simple structure on the latent space, which may not capture complex reward landscapes.
Gradient-based saliency is only applied to the Stop action, missing intermediate decision points.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to multi-objective settings such as synthetic accessibility or binding affinity.
Condition GFlowNets directly on physicochemical properties for more interpretable representations.
Investigate the impact of interpretability tools on downstream molecule design and compare with alternative methods.
papers.abstract: Generative Flow Networks, or GFlowNets, offer a promising framework for molecular design, but their internal decision policies remain opaque. This limits adoption in drug discovery, where chemists require clear and interpretable rationales for proposed structures. We present an interpretability framework for SynFlowNet, a GFlowNet trained on documented chemical reactions and purchasable starting materials that generates both molecules and the synthetic routes that produce them. Our approach integrates three complementary components. Gradient based saliency combined with counterfactual perturbations identifies which atomic environments influence reward and how structural edits change molecular outcomes. Sparse autoencoders reveal axis aligned latent factors that correspond to physicochemical properties such as polarity, lipophilicity, and molecular size. Motif probes show that functional groups including aromatic rings and halogens are explicitly encoded and linearly decodable from the internal embeddings. Together, these results expose the chemical logic inside SynFlowNet and provide actionable and mechanistic insight that supports transparent and controllable molecular design.

papers.title: Systematic Evaluation of Single-Cell Foundation Model Interpretability Reveals Attention Captures Co-Expression Rather Than Unique Regulatory Signal
papers.research_question: Does attention in single-cell foundation models capture causal regulatory relationships or just co-expression? Do attention-derived edge scores provide incremental value beyond gene-level features for predicting perturbation outcomes?
papers.core_contribution: Attention patterns in single-cell foundation models encode structured biological information (e.g., protein-protein interactions in early layers, transcriptional regulation in late layers) but do not capture causal regulatory signal; they provide no incremental value over gene-level features for predicting perturbation outcomes.
papers.conclusion: Attention patterns in single-cell foundation models capture co-expression rather than causal regulatory signal, and the proposed evaluation framework provides a reusable quality-control standard for mechanistic interpretability in this domain.
papers.key_findings:
Attention patterns show layer-specific biological specialization but do not outperform trivial gene-level baselines for perturbation prediction.
Pairwise edge scores (attention or correlation) provide no incremental predictive value beyond gene-level features.
Causal ablation of 'regulatory' attention heads does not degrade perturbation prediction, indicating distributed redundancy.
The relationship between attention and correlation is context-dependent across cell types and perturbation modalities.
Cell-State Stratified Interpretability (CSSI) improves attention-derived GRN recovery by controlling for heterogeneity.
papers.limitation:
Causal ablation only performed on Geneformer V2-316M, not on scGPT due to architectural differences.
Perturbation data limited to four cell types and two modalities; additional tissues, species, and architectures remain untested.
No decisive positive control demonstrates recovery of known causal regulatory structure in a realistic perturbation setting.
future_direction: Test additional tissues, species, and architectures (e.g., scFoundation).
Focus interpretability efforts on residual-stream geometry, MLP-stored knowledge, or representations from the full forward pass.
papers.abstract: We present a systematic evaluation framework - thirty-seven analyses, 153 statistical tests, four cell types, two perturbation modalities - for assessing mechanistic interpretability in single-cell foundation models. Applying this framework to scGPT and Geneformer, we find that attention patterns encode structured biological information with layer-specific organisation - protein-protein interactions in early layers, transcriptional regulation in late layers - but this structure provides no incremental value for perturbation prediction: trivial gene-level baselines outperform both attention and correlation edges (AUROC 0.81-0.88 versus 0.70), pairwise edge scores add zero predictive contribution, and causal ablation of regulatory heads produces no degradation. These findings generalise from K562 to RPE1 cells; the attention-correlation relationship is context-dependent, but gene-level dominance is universal. Cell-State Stratified Interpretability (CSSI) addresses an attention-specific scaling failure, improving GRN recovery up to 1.85x. The framework establishes reusable quality-control standards for the field.

papers.title: Insights on representational similarity in neural networks with canonical correlation
papers.research_question: How can we compare neural network representations and understand their evolution over time? The paper develops projection weighted CCA to address this.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces projection weighted CCA, an improved method for comparing neural network representations, and uses it to show that generalizing networks converge to more similar representations than memorizing networks, wider networks converge to more similar solutions, and RNNs exhibit bottom-up convergence during training.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that projection weighted CCA is a useful tool for analyzing neural network representations, revealing insights about convergence and similarity across networks and over time.
papers.key_findings:
Networks that generalize converge to more similar representations than those that memorize.
Wider networks converge to more similar solutions than narrower networks.
Networks with identical topology but different learning rates converge to distinct clusters of solutions.
RNNs exhibit bottom-up convergence over the course of training.
RNN hidden states vary nonlinearly across sequence timesteps, even when accounting for linear transforms.
future_direction: Examine what is unique about directions preserved across networks trained with different initializations.
Explore whether the insight about similarity and generalization could be used as a regularizer to improve network performance.
Investigate which aspects of RNN representations are stable over time and which vary.
papers.abstract: Comparing different neural network representations and determining how representations evolve over time remain challenging open questions in our understanding of the function of neural networks. Comparing representations in neural networks is fundamentally difficult as the structure of representations varies greatly, even across groups of networks trained on identical tasks, and over the course of training. Here, we develop projection weighted CCA (Canonical Correlation Analysis) as a tool for understanding neural networks, building off of SVCCA, a recently proposed method (Raghu et al., 2017). We first improve the core method, showing how to differentiate between signal and noise, and then apply this technique to compare across a group of CNNs, demonstrating that networks which generalize converge to more similar representations than networks which memorize, that wider networks converge to more similar solutions than narrow networks, and that trained networks with identical topology but different learning rates converge to distinct clusters with diverse representations. We also investigate the representational dynamics of RNNs, across both training and sequential timesteps, finding that RNNs converge in a bottom-up pattern over the course of training and that the hidden state is highly variable over the course of a sequence, even when accounting for linear transforms. Together, these results provide new insights into the function of CNNs and RNNs, and demonstrate the utility of using CCA to understand representations.

papers.title: What Has a Foundation Model Found? Using Inductive Bias to Probe for World Models
papers.research_question: Does a foundation model's inductive bias align with a postulated world model, indicating that it has learned deeper structure from sequence prediction?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an inductive bias probe to evaluate whether foundation models have learned a postulated world model, and finds that they often fail to do so, instead developing task-specific heuristics.
papers.conclusion: The inductive bias probe reveals that foundation models often fail to learn the underlying world models, instead relying on task-specific heuristics, which limits their generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Foundation models trained on orbital trajectories fail to apply Newtonian mechanics when adapted to new physics tasks.
Models behave as if they develop task-specific heuristics that fail to generalize.
In lattice and Othello, models have an inductive bias toward legal next-tokens rather than the world model.
Models that perform better on inductive bias probes have better transfer performance on new tasks that rely on the underlying world model.
LLMs also fail to predict force magnitudes accurately in physics tasks.
papers.limitation: Fine-tuning proprietary LLMs is infeasible and running the full inductive bias probe is expensive.
papers.abstract: Foundation models are premised on the idea that sequence prediction can uncover deeper domain understanding, much like how Kepler's predictions of planetary motion later led to the discovery of Newtonian mechanics. However, evaluating whether these models truly capture deeper structure remains a challenge. We develop a technique for evaluating foundation models that examines how they adapt to synthetic datasets generated from some postulated world model. Our technique measures whether the foundation model's inductive bias aligns with the world model, and so we refer to it as an inductive bias probe. Across multiple domains, we find that foundation models can excel at their training tasks yet fail to develop inductive biases towards the underlying world model when adapted to new tasks. We particularly find that foundation models trained on orbital trajectories consistently fail to apply Newtonian mechanics when adapted to new physics tasks. Further analysis reveals that these models behave as if they develop task-specific heuristics that fail to generalize.

papers.title: BERT Learns (and Teaches) Chemistry
papers.research_question: Can attention mechanisms in BERT be used to identify important molecular substructures (functional groups) from SMILES string representations and apply these learned representations to chemical property prediction tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that BERT's attention mechanisms can identify chemically relevant functional groups from SMILES strings without domain heuristics, and that these learned representations can be applied to downstream chemical property prediction tasks.
papers.conclusion: Attention visualization in BERT provides a data-driven method to identify functional groups and important molecular substructures from SMILES strings, offering a potentially useful tool for computational chemistry despite not achieving state-of-the-art performance on downstream tasks.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's attention heads, trained only on SMILES strings, learn to attend to atoms that correspond to known active reaction sites (functional groups) in molecules, even without explicit reaction data.
When fine-tuned on chemical property regression tasks (e.g., solubility), specific attention heads in BERT focus on relevant substructures (e.g., carbon chains for solubility).
Using BERT embeddings as features for graph models (GCN, GAT) on toxicity prediction tasks yields competitive but not state-of-the-art performance compared to canonical atom featurization.
Attention visualization of BERT trained on chemical data can serve as a tool for chemistry practitioners to quickly identify important substructures related to various chemical properties.
papers.limitation:
BERT embeddings did not improve upon the state of the art when used as features for graph models on toxicity prediction; the learned information appears to be a subset of that captured by canonical atom featurization.
Some molecules in the Tox21 dataset contain atoms not present in BERT's vocabulary, which may detract from performance.
Attention heads after fine-tuning on most chemical property tasks (QED, SAS) showed little change from pretraining, except for the solubility task, suggesting the fine-tuning may find a local optimum close to pretraining weights.
future_direction: Using a larger dataset of 96 million molecules from PubMed to train BERT, given that language models thrive with abundant data.
Designing a loss function that penalizes distances between embeddings of different SMILES strings representing the same molecule to force BERT to learn the inherent graphical meaning.
Further investigating the approach of analyzing chemical property-bearing molecular substructures via fine-tuning to make it a more useful tool for chemists.
papers.abstract: Modern computational organic chemistry is becoming increasingly data-driven. There remain a large number of important unsolved problems in this area such as product prediction given reactants, drug discovery, and metric-optimized molecule synthesis, but efforts to solve these problems using machine learning have also increased in recent years. In this work, we propose the use of attention to study functional groups and other property-impacting molecular substructures from a data-driven perspective, using a transformer-based model (BERT) on datasets of string representations of molecules and analyzing the behavior of its attention heads. We then apply the representations of functional groups and atoms learned by the model to tackle problems of toxicity, solubility, drug-likeness, and synthesis accessibility on smaller datasets using the learned representations as features for graph convolution and attention models on the graph structure of molecules, as well as fine-tuning of BERT. Finally, we propose the use of attention visualization as a helpful tool for chemistry practitioners and students to quickly identify important substructures in various chemical properties.

papers.title: Convergent Learning: Do different neural networks learn the same representations?
papers.research_question: Do different neural networks with the same architecture trained from different random initializations learn the same representations (i.e., exhibit convergent learning)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces methods to compare neural network representations and shows that networks exhibit partial convergent learning, with some features learned reliably across networks and others not, and that representations are a mix of local and slightly distributed codes.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks exhibit convergent learning to some extent, and the introduced methods are effective for understanding and comparing the representations they learn.
papers.key_findings:
Some features are learned reliably in multiple networks, yet other features are not consistently learned.
Units learn to span low-dimensional subspaces and, while these subspaces are common to multiple networks, the specific basis vectors learned are not.
The representation codes show evidence of being a mix between a local (single unit) code and slightly, but not fully, distributed codes across multiple units.
The average activation values of neurons vary considerably within a network, yet the mean activation values across different networks converge to an almost identical distribution.
Features learned in different networks are most convergent on the first convolutional layer (conv1) and least convergent on the fourth (conv4).
papers.limitation: Mapping layers for higher layers (conv3-conv5) showed poor performance, and the reasons are not fully understood.
future_direction: Investigate different architectures, training algorithms, and hyperparameters.
Train more powerful predictive models for higher layers with different hyperparameters or architectures.
papers.abstract: Recent success in training deep neural networks have prompted active investigation into the features learned on their intermediate layers. Such research is difficult because it requires making sense of non-linear computations performed by millions of parameters, but valuable because it increases our ability to understand current models and create improved versions of them. In this paper we investigate the extent to which neural networks exhibit what we call convergent learning, which is when the representations learned by multiple nets converge to a set of features which are either individually similar between networks or where subsets of features span similar low-dimensional spaces. We propose a specific method of probing representations: training multiple networks and then comparing and contrasting their individual, learned representations at the level of neurons or groups of neurons. We begin research into this question using three techniques to approximately align different neural networks on a feature level: a bipartite matching approach that makes one-to-one assignments between neurons, a sparse prediction approach that finds one-to-many mappings, and a spectral clustering approach that finds many-to-many mappings. This initial investigation reveals a few previously unknown properties of neural networks, and we argue that future research into the question of convergent learning will yield many more. The insights described here include (1) that some features are learned reliably in multiple networks, yet other features are not consistently learned; (2) that units learn to span low-dimensional subspaces and, while these subspaces are common to multiple networks, the specific basis vectors learned are not; (3) that the representation codes show evidence of being a mix between a local code and slightly, but not fully, distributed codes across multiple units.

papers.title: Activation function dependence of the storage capacity of treelike neural networks
papers.research_question: How does the activation function affect the storage capacity of treelike neural networks, and under what conditions does the capacity remain finite in the infinite-width limit?
papers.core_contribution: The storage capacity of treelike committee machines remains finite in the infinite-width limit if and only if the activation function is weakly differentiable with square-integrable derivative, and nonlinearity can increase capacity but reduce classification robustness.
papers.conclusion: The results elucidate how activation function smoothness affects storage capacity and robustness, and generate a hypothesis for the functional benefit of dendritic spikes in biological neurons.
papers.key_findings:
The capacity remains finite in the infinite-width limit for activation functions in the Sobolev class H1(γ) (weakly differentiable with square-integrable derivative).
For sign activation, capacity diverges; for ReLU, erf, tanh, quadratic, etc., capacity is finite.
Nonlinearity increases the zero-margin capacity but can reduce the large-margin capacity, potentially reducing robustness.
Explicit capacity formulas are derived for common activation functions: ReLU (α_RS = 2π/(π-1) ≈ 2.93), erf (α_RS ≈ 2.45), quadratic (α_RS = 4).
Replica symmetry breaking reduces capacity estimates but preserves the ordering across activation functions.
papers.limitation:
The replica method lacks rigorous justification for all cases, and the capacity results may not be provably correct.
The Gardner volume approach is agnostic to learning algorithms, so it does not guarantee that solutions can be found in practice.
future_direction: Investigate how other forms of data structure affect storage capacity.
Test the hypothesis about dendritic spikes using more biophysically realistic models.
Extend the analysis to fully-connected committee machines.
papers.abstract: The expressive power of artificial neural networks crucially depends on the nonlinearity of their activation functions. Though a wide variety of nonlinear activation functions have been proposed for use in artificial neural networks, a detailed understanding of their role in determining the expressive power of a network has not emerged. Here, we study how activation functions affect the storage capacity of treelike two-layer networks. We relate the boundedness or divergence of the capacity in the infinite-width limit to the smoothness of the activation function, elucidating the relationship between previously studied special cases. Our results show that nonlinearity can both increase capacity and decrease the robustness of classification, and provide simple estimates for the capacity of networks with several commonly used activation functions. Furthermore, they generate a hypothesis for the functional benefit of dendritic spikes in branched neurons.

papers.title: An Investigation of Interpretability Techniques for Deep Learning in Predictive Process Analytics
papers.research_question: Do patients with specific types of cancer have a targeted set of medical activities associated with them? What explainability mechanisms are appropriate for understanding predictions in this context?
papers.core_contribution: This paper applies interpretability techniques (autoencoders and LIME) to deep learning and random forest models on medical event logs, providing insights into cancer prediction and model decisions.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability techniques like autoencoders and LIME can provide meaningful insights into model predictions for medical event logs, aiding in understanding and trust.
papers.key_findings:
LSTM neural networks achieved the best accuracy (0.552) for cancer prediction from medical event logs.
Autoencoders applied to hidden layers of LSTM networks revealed non-linear clusters corresponding to cancer types, helping identify misclassifications.
LIME provided local explanations for random forest predictions, highlighting features like age and specific activities as important for individual predictions.
Both autoencoders and LIME offered complementary interpretability insights: autoencoders via non-linear cluster representations and LIME via local feature impact.
papers.limitation:
The dataset is small (1142 patients) and models show overfitting.
Non-linear projections in autoencoders can distort distances, leading to misclassifications.
papers.abstract: This paper explores interpretability techniques for two of the most successful learning algorithms in medical decision-making literature: deep neural networks and random forests. We applied these algorithms in a real-world medical dataset containing information about patients with cancer, where we learn models that try to predict the type of cancer of the patient, given their set of medical activity records. We explored different algorithms based on neural network architectures using long short term deep neural networks, and random forests. Since there is a growing need to provide decision-makers understandings about the logic of predictions of black boxes, we also explored different techniques that provide interpretations for these classifiers. In one of the techniques, we intercepted some hidden layers of these neural networks and used autoencoders in order to learn what is the representation of the input in the hidden layers. In another, we investigated an interpretable model locally around the random forest's prediction. Results show learning an interpretable model locally around the model's prediction leads to a higher understanding of why the algorithm is making some decision. Use of local and linear model helps identify the features used in prediction of a specific instance or data point. We see certain distinct features used for predictions that provide useful insights about the type of cancer, along with features that do not generalize well. In addition, the structured deep learning approach using autoencoders provided meaningful prediction insights, which resulted in the identification of nonlinear clusters correspondent to the patients' different types of cancer.

papers.title: Analysis of a convolutional neural network for predicting unsteady volume wake flow fields
papers.research_question: How does a convolutional neural network system learn and predict three-dimensional unsteady wake flow dynamics in different flow regimes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops a multi-scale CNN system for predicting 3D unsteady wake flow and investigates its mechanisms, showing that convolution layers integrate and transport wavenumber information to extract flow structures, and that redundant feature maps can be identified and removed to reduce model size without loss of performance.
papers.conclusion: The CNN system predicts wake flow by integrating and transporting wavenumber information through convolution layers, extracting representations of flow dynamics. Redundant feature maps can be removed based on structural similarity, significantly reducing model size without performance loss.
papers.key_findings:
The CNN system predicts flow in different regimes by transporting wavenumber information through convolution layers.
Feature maps extract similar flow structures (e.g., braid shear layers and shedding vortices) across different Reynolds numbers.
Convolution layers integrate information from all input flow variables and histories, with more recent histories having larger contributions.
Redundant feature maps can be identified using structural similarity (SSIM) and removed, reducing the number of weights by 85% without affecting prediction performance.
papers.abstract: A predictive convolutional neural network is developed to predict the future of three-dimensional unsteady wake flow from past information of flow velocity and pressure. The developed network is found to be capable of predicting vortex dynamics at distinctive flow regimes with flow structures at different scales. Mechanisms of the network on predicting vortex dynamics at two distinctive flow regimes, the mode-B shedding regime and the turbulent wake regime, are investigated. Information in feature maps of the network is visualized and quantitatively assessed to investigate the encoded flow structures. A Fourier analysis is conducted to investigate the mechanisms of the network on learning fluid motions with distinctive flow scales. The transformation of information from the input to prediction layers of the network is tracked to examine how the network transforms the input information for prediction. Structural similarities among feature maps in the network are evaluated to reduce the number of feature maps containing redundant flow structures, which allows reduction of the size of the network without affecting prediction performance.

papers.title: Tensor Product Decomposition Networks: Uncovering Representations of Structure Learned by Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How do neural networks encode compositional symbolic structure in their vector representations, and do they use tensor product representations?
papers.core_contribution: TPDNs show that RNNs can learn structured representations similar to tensor product representations for artificial tasks, but for real-world NLP tasks, representations are less structured, approximated by bag-of-words, suggesting training tasks may not induce robust structural representations.
papers.conclusion: RNNs trained on structure-sensitive tasks learn representations well approximated by tensor-product representations, but sentence encoders for NLP tasks show less structure, approximated by bag-of-words.
papers.key_findings:
TPDNs can closely approximate RNN representations for digit sequence copying tasks, indicating structured encoding.
Linear RNNs use bidirectional role schemes, while tree RNNs use tree position roles for representation.
For natural language processing models like InferSent and Skip-thought, representations are well approximated by bag-of-words, showing limited structure.
The nature of learned representations is related to the RNN's structure and the training task.
Training tasks influence whether networks discover structured or unstructured representations.
papers.abstract: We introduce an analysis technique for understanding compositional structure present in the vector representations used by neural networks. The inner workings of neural networks are notoriously difficult to understand, and in particular it is far from clear how they manage to perform remarkably well on tasks that depend on compositional structure even though they use continuous vector representations with no obvious compositional structure. Using our analysis technique, we show that the representations of these models can be closely approximated by Tensor Product Representations, a type of interpretable structure that lends significant insight into the workings of these hard-to-interpret models.

papers.title: Cellular automata as convolutional neural networks
papers.research_question: How do neural networks encode and represent dynamical rules, specifically in the context of cellular automata?
papers.core_contribution: Shows that convolutional neural networks can represent and learn arbitrary cellular automata rules, and that the internal representations of trained networks reflect the complexity (entropy) of the CA rules.
papers.conclusion: Convolutional neural networks can learn cellular automata rules, and the complexity of the rules affects the depth and specialization of the learned representations, suggesting that the entropy of a physical process can affect its representation when learned by neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
Any cellular automaton can be represented by a convolutional neural network with a network-in-network architecture.
A general convolutional multilayer perceptron architecture can learn arbitrary CA rules when given videos of the CA as training data.
In the limit of large network widths, training dynamics are nearly identical across replicates.
Cellular automata with simpler rule tables produce trained networks with hierarchical structure and layer specialization, while more complex CA produce shallower representations.
The entropy of the CA rule table influences the specificity of the internal representations in the trained network.
future_direction: Determine whether neural networks can more broadly inform efforts to understand the dynamical space of CA, including relating a CA's a priori rules to its apparent dynamical complexity during simulation.
Relate observations to more general patterns in deep networks, such as the information bottleneck.
papers.abstract: Deep-learning techniques have recently demonstrated broad success in predicting complex dynamical systems ranging from turbulence to human speech, motivating broader questions about how neural networks encode and represent dynamical rules. We explore this problem in the context of cellular automata (CA), simple dynamical systems that are intrinsically discrete and thus difficult to analyze using standard tools from dynamical systems theory. We show that any CA may readily be represented using a convolutional neural network with a network-in-network architecture. This motivates the development of a general convolutional multilayer perceptron architecture, which we find can learn the dynamical rules for arbitrary CA when given videos of the CA as training data. In the limit of large network widths, we find that training dynamics are nearly identical across replicates, and that common patterns emerge in the structure of networks trained on different CA rulesets. We train ensembles of networks on randomly sampled CA, and we probe how the trained networks internally represent the CA rules using an information-theoretic technique based on distributions of layer activation patterns. We find that CA with simpler rule tables produce trained networks with hierarchical structure and layer specialization, while more complex CA produce shallower representations-illustrating how the underlying complexity of the CA's rules influences the specificity of these internal representations. Our results suggest how the entropy of a physical process can affect its representation when learned by neural networks.

papers.title: Exploring the balance between interpretability and performance with carefully designed constrainable Neural Additive Models
papers.research_question: How can we explore the balance between model interpretability and performance by introducing a constrainable Neural Additive Model (CNAM) that allows joint optimization of both objectives?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Constrainable Neural Additive Models (CNAM), a novel formulation of Neural Additive Models that allows the specification of interpretability constraints (e.g., monotonicity, smoothness, sparsity) to be jointly optimized with task performance, enabling exploration of the interpretability-performance tradeoff.
papers.conclusion: CNAM is an effective method for explicitly exploring the trade-off between interpretability and performance in neural additive models, providing a flexible framework that can be initialized from efficient solvers and optimized under various interpretability constraints.
papers.key_findings:
CNAM, when initialized from EBM solutions and optimized with different regularizations, produces models that lie on the Pareto front of optimal solutions in terms of interpretability (SHAP-Length) and performance (e.g., ROC AUC, Accuracy, F1-Score, R2).
CNAM can achieve similar performance to Logistic Regression while being roughly twice as interpretable (in terms of SHAP-Length) on regression tasks, and can also find solutions with significantly better performance than Logistic Regression while maintaining similar interpretability.
The model's structure, based on differentiable steps, allows for easy initialization from tree-based GAM solvers like EBM and the enforcement of various constraints through additional loss terms.
Empirical benchmarking on 56 binary classification datasets shows that CNAM variants, on average, rank on the Pareto front when considering both interpretability and performance metrics.
CNAM is applicable to both classification and regression tasks, providing interpretable shape functions for each feature that can be visualized and constrained.
papers.limitation:
The SHAP-Length metric used to measure interpretability might not be the ideal measure for all use cases; future developments might yield alternative metrics better suited for specific contexts or expert preferences.
CNAM is restricted to univariate feature modeling, disregarding higher-order feature interactions, which limits expressiveness when faced with complex feature interactions.
Applying CNAM to other data types (e.g., images, text, time series) requires representing these data in an interpretable tabular format through feature engineering, which may not always yield coherent explanations.
future_direction: Integrate CNAM with GAM-changer to enable a feedback loop between the model and the user for iterative refinement of performance and interpretability objectives.
Explore more intelligent search techniques, such as multiobjective metaheuristics, to improve the model's capability in searching for better tradeoffs in the Pareto space.

Investigate the efficient creation of counterfactual explanations by exploiting the specific structure of CNAM, and explore enabling pairwise interactions to boost task performance (at the cost of harder interpretability).
papers.abstract: The interpretability of an intelligent model automatically derived from data is a property that can be acted upon with a set of structural constraints that such a model should adhere to. Often these are in contrast with the task objective and it is not straightforward how to explore the balance between model interpretability and performance. In order to allow an interested user to jointly optimise performance and interpretability, we propose a new formulation of Neural Additive Models (NAM) which can be subject to a number of constraints. Accordingly, our approach produces a new model that is called Constrainable NAM (or just CNAM in short) and it allows the specification of different regularisation terms. CNAM is differentiable and is built in such a way that it can be initialised as a solution of an efficient tree-based GAM solver (e.g., Explainable Boosting Machines). From this local optimum the model can then explore solutions with different interpretability-performance tradeoffs according to different definitions of both interpretability and performance. We empirically benchmark the model on 56 datasets against 12 models and observe that on average the proposed CNAM model ranks on the Pareto front of optimal solutions, i.e., models generated by CNAM exhibit a good balance between interpretability and performance. Moreover, we provide two illustrative examples which are aimed to show step by step how CNAM works well for solving classification tasks, but also how it can yield insights when considering regression tasks.

papers.title: The Next Five Hurdles What is a Linear Representation? What is a Multidimensional Feature? The Dark Matter of Neural Networks? Attention Pivot Tables Measuring feature sensitivity using dataset filtering
papers.research_question: What are the major hurdles facing mechanistic interpretability, and how can we improve feature analysis and measurement?
papers.core_contribution: This blog post outlines five key hurdles in mechanistic interpretability, refines the concept of linear representations to include multidimensional features, introduces the idea of 'dark matter' features, provides practical guidance for using attention pivot tables, and demonstrates a method to measure feature sensitivity using LLM-assisted dataset filtering.
papers.conclusion: The authors are optimistic about progress in mechanistic interpretability despite challenges, and highlight the need for further research into feature cooperation and improved analysis methods.
papers.key_findings:
Current sparse autoencoder methods may miss many rare features, suggesting a 'dark matter' of neural networks that is difficult to observe.
Linear representations can be mathematically linear even with multidimensional features, requiring a revised definition.
Attention pivot tables reveal interpretable skip-trigrams in one-layer transformers, but their clarity depends on training details and dataset.
Feature sensitivity measured via Claude-filtered datasets shows that individual features often have low sensitivity, and concepts are represented by multiple cooperating features.
Different versions of Claude agree well with each other and with human judgments when rating concept relevance in text snippets.
papers.limitation:
Dictionary learning may be unable to resolve extremely rare features, limiting comprehensiveness.
Features identified by sparse autoencoders often have imperfect sensitivity and specificity, with concepts distributed across multiple features.
Attention pivot table results are sensitive to training hyperparameters and dataset composition, making interpretation unreliable under suboptimal conditions.
future_direction: Developing more efficient dictionary learning algorithms to capture rare features.
Automating the discovery of complementary features that collectively represent concepts.
Further investigation into attention superposition and cross-layer superposition.
papers.abstract: What are the major hurdles facing mechanistic interpretability, and how can we improve feature analysis and measurement? This blog post outlines five key hurdles in mechanistic interpretability, refines the concept of linear representations to include multidimensional features, introduces the idea of 'dark matter' features, provides practical guidance for using attention pivot tables, and demonstrates a method to measure feature sensitivity using LLM-assisted dataset filtering. The authors are optimistic about progress in mechanistic interpretability despite challenges, and highlight the need for further research into feature cooperation and improved analysis methods.

papers.title: Open Roles In Interpretability Scaling Laws for Dictionary Learning Update on how we train SAEs How Strongly do Dictionary Learning Features Influence Model Behavior? Interpretability Architectures Project Caloric and the Utility of Incorrect Theories Open Problem: Attribution Dictionary Learning Isolating Circuits Paths of Different Lengths
papers.core_contribution: This blog post reports several developments in mechanistic interpretability, including scaling laws for dictionary learning, updates on SAE training techniques, and preliminary evidence that dictionary learning features significantly influence model behavior.
papers.conclusion: The updates demonstrate progress in dictionary learning and circuit analysis, with SAE features showing causal influence on model behavior, and open problems like attribution dictionary learning offering directions for further research.
papers.key_findings:
Scaling laws for dictionary learning show that loss decreases approximately as a power law with compute, with optimal allocations of training steps and features scaling as power laws.
An improved SAE training setup with modified loss function and initialization reduces loss and allows scaling to millions of features without issues.
Ablating dictionary learning features causes significantly more loss increase than random perturbations, indicating that features are high-leverage for model behavior.
Feature ablations have a larger effect than feature doublings, suggesting that feature influence may saturate at higher activations.
The impact of feature ablations is more pronounced for residual stream features compared to MLP features, hinting at different functional roles.
papers.limitation:
The relationship between SAE loss and qualitative usefulness of SAE features is imperfect and may break down at sufficient scale.
The SAE training initialization may need improvement and could cause issues for large feature counts.
The results on feature influence are preliminary and require further investigation.
future_direction: Exploring interpretable model architectures
Investigating attribution dictionary learning
Improving SAE training methods such as initialization and post-training
papers.abstract: This blog post reports several developments in mechanistic interpretability, including scaling laws for dictionary learning, updates on SAE training techniques, and preliminary evidence that dictionary learning features significantly influence model behavior. The updates demonstrate progress in dictionary learning and circuit analysis, with SAE features showing causal influence on model behavior, and open problems like attribution dictionary learning offering directions for further research.

papers.title: TIME: A Transparent, Interpretable, Model-Adaptive and Explainable Neural Network for Dynamic Physical Processes
papers.research_question: Can we recover an invariant structure (PDE) from dense space-time observations, detect anomalies, and make the network interpretable and transparent?
papers.core_contribution: A low-weight, fully convolutional encoder-decoder network that learns interpretable representations of PDEs from space-time data, with transparency and explainability.
papers.conclusion: The TIME network is effective for learning PDE representations and provides interpretability and explainability, allowing modelers to verify the network's workings against their domain knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
The network can learn PDE kernels that approximate differential operators.
Network design (depth and number of kernels) affects interpretability and accuracy.
The network is robust to scaling and can detect missing data as anomalies in activation maps.
A compact representation (appropriate depth and kernel count) performs best while maintaining interpretability.
High-weight representations are redundant and impact interpretability.
future_direction: Imbibe complicated processes with additional domain constraints.
papers.abstract: Partial Differential Equations are infinite dimensional encoded representations of physical processes. However, imbibing multiple observation data towards a coupled representation presents significant challenges. We present a fully convolutional architecture that captures the invariant structure of the domain to reconstruct the observable system. The proposed architecture is significantly low-weight compared to other networks for such problems. Our intent is to learn coupled dynamic processes interpreted as deviations from true kernels representing isolated processes for model-adaptivity.
